questions.title: Ciphertext
questions.q: Cipher text is the scrambled and unreadable output of encryption.
questions.answer: TRUE. Encryption transforms plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key. Decryption recovers plaintext using the appropriate key. Hashing instead produces a digest for comparison and has no decryption operation.
questions.teach: Plaintext is the readable message. Ciphertext is its encrypted representation. A digest is a different kind of output.
questions.example: A payroll file is encrypted before transfer. Someone who intercepts the file sees ciphertext and needs the appropriate decryption key to read it.
questions.correct: True
distractors: False
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Ciphertext in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: False

questions.title: Targets beyond payment data
questions.q: Attackers target personal information beyond credit-card numbers and bank-account numbers to make money. True or false?
questions.answer: CC means credit card. The # symbol means number here: CC# means credit-card number, and bank account# means bank-account number. The statement says criminals also profit from other personal information, such as passwords, identity details, and medical records. TRUE. Personal information, credentials, health records, private communications, and intellectual property can support fraud, extortion, resale, and espionage. The textbook’s social-engineering example shows why account-recovery information can be valuable even without a full card number.

questions.title: SET and stealth
questions.q: SET-based attack has become more popular these days due to its stealthy penetration.
questions.answer: TRUE. SET (Social Engineer Toolkit) means Social-Engineer Toolkit. Your SET (Social Engineer Toolkit) lab shows that a convincing fake login page can capture credentials through user interaction, and a redirect can conceal the deception. The key concept is social engineering: deception persuades the user to disclose information, reducing the attacker’s dependence on exploiting a software vulnerability.
questions.teach: A user trusts a deceptive page and submits credentials. A familiar appearance and a redirect to the real site can make the credential theft less noticeable.
questions.example: A fully patched employee enters a password on a cloned login page. The password is disclosed without exploiting a software flaw. Login monitoring and phishing-resistant MFA (Multi Factor Authentication) reduce the resulting risk.
questions.correct: True
distractors: False because SET cannot collect credentials
True because SET always bypasses every control
False because SET is an encryption algorithm
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage

questions.title: Reverse shell and firewall limits
questions.q: The reverse shell attack is capable of defeating packet filtering firewall but not proxy firewall.
questions.answer: FALSE as written. A reverse shell starts an outbound connection from a compromised internal host to an attacker. It can pass packet filters that allow that outbound traffic. A proxy can require authentication, restrict destinations and protocols, and inspect traffic, but its effectiveness depends on configuration and visibility. A properly configured proxy can block a raw shell connection by enforcing application protocols. A shell tunneled through an allowed application protocol still requires inspection and policy enforcement; the word proxy alone does not guarantee prevention.
questions.teach: Direction and policy explain the result. Outbound does not mean automatically allowed, and proxy does not mean automatically secure.
questions.example: A workstation makes an unusual outbound connection after a malicious process starts. Correlate process and network logs, isolate the host, and restrict unnecessary egress rather than relying solely on inbound rules.
questions.correct: False: firewall effectiveness depends on its rules and inspection
distractors: Always true for every proxy
False because reverse shells only start inbound connections
True because a proxy encrypts every endpoint process
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage

questions.title: TCP/IP is a suite
questions.q: TCP/IP represent a suite of protocols including DNS, SNMP, SMPT, POP, and FTP etc.
questions.answer: TRUE with a spelling correction: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), not SMPT. TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol) names a protocol suite spanning layers. DNS (Domain Name System) resolves names, SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) supports device management, SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) transfers mail, POP (Post Office Protocol) retrieves mail, and FTP (File Transfer Protocol) transfers files. They are not all transport-layer protocols.
questions.teach: The suite is the whole family. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and IP (Internet Protocol) are central members with different jobs.
questions.example: A mail application resolves a server name with DNS (Domain Name System), connects using transport protocols, and uses SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) to send mail. Several suite members cooperate.
questions.correct: True
distractors: False
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol) is a suite in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: False

questions.title: Race condition
questions.q: What is a race condition?
questions.answer: D. Concurrent execution accesses shared state without adequate synchronization, so the result depends on timing or ordering and can become unintended. A race condition is a concurrency flaw, not a synonym for DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service), slow processing, or a race to patch before attackers act.
questions.teach: Two operations interfere because each assumes it can use the same state safely. Locking, atomic operations, or safe transaction design can prevent this.
questions.example: Two checkout requests both see one remaining item before either updates stock. Both complete, selling the same item twice.
questions.correct: Concurrent execution accesses a shared resource and causes unintended consequences
distractors: A race to patch a newly discovered vulnerability
A software update released before discovery
An attack finishing before antivirus scanning
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Race condition in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A race to patch a newly discovered vulnerability

setting.location: Concurrent operations in the store’s application and shared stock record.
setting.purpose: Prevent conflicting operations from producing an unintended result. If both requests read the old stock value before either updates it, timing can cause an incorrect result. Safe synchronization or transactions address the race.
setting.action: If both requests read the old stock value before either updates it, timing can cause an incorrect result. Safe synchronization or transactions address the race.

questions.title: Vishing
questions.q: Which statement is correct about vishing?
questions.answer: C. VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) makes caller-ID spoofing easier. Vishing is voice phishing: an attacker uses a call or voice message to trick someone into revealing information or performing an action. Calls can be automated, targeted, or broadly distributed; it does not always require a live person.
questions.teach: Voice is the identifying feature. Caller ID is a claim, not proof of identity.
questions.example: A caller claims to be the help desk and asks for a login code. Hang up and verify through an independently known help-desk number.
questions.correct: VoIP makes caller-ID spoofing easier
distractors: It is only tailored to organizations
It only targets large organizations
It always uses a real person to call

questions.title: Email sender investigation
questions.q: To investigate a phishing email, where would you go for sender information?
questions.answer: D. Email header. Full headers provide routing and sender-related fields such as Received, Return-Path, and authentication results. Compare these with the claimed sender and timestamps. A display name, body, attachment, or embedded URL (Uniform Resource Locator) alone does not establish who sent the message. Some header fields can also be forged; establish trusted receiving-system boundaries.
questions.teach: Headers provide evidence for investigation. Reading the visible sender label alone is not enough.
questions.example: An email claims to come from campus IT (Information Technology) but uses a lookalike domain and urgent password language. Preserve the message and inspect headers through the approved reporting process.
questions.correct: Email header
distractors: Attachment
Embedded URL
Email body

questions.title: Static analysis terminology
questions.q: Which of the following is a static analysis tool: Firebug, McAfee Advisor, JSUnpack, Norton SafeWeb, or OpenSSL?
questions.answer: C. JSUnpack. It unpacks and analyzes suspicious JavaScript to expose concealed code and URLs. Remember the underlying distinction: static analysis inspects code without running it; dynamic analysis observes execution. JSUnpack also uses emulation, so its capabilities extend beyond static inspection. Firebug is a browser debugger, SiteAdvisor and Safe Web are reputation services, and OpenSSL is a cryptographic toolkit. Static analysis examines code without executing it; dynamic analysis observes execution.
questions.teach: Associate JSUnpack with unpacking suspicious JavaScript. Static versus dynamic describes whether code executes; manual versus automated describes who or what performs the analysis.
questions.example: Reading script text and decoding an embedded string without running the script is static work. Observing redirects while script executes in an isolated environment is dynamic work.
questions.correct: JSUnpack
distractors: McAfee Advisor is a source-code compiler
Norton SafeWeb is an offline disassembler
OpenSSL is a browser reputation database
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Static analysis terminology in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: McAfee Advisor is a source-code compiler

questions.title: TCP reliability
questions.q: Which protocol is responsible for data packet quality and basic security features in transmission?
questions.answer: A. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol). Transmission Control Protocol provides reliable, ordered byte-stream delivery using acknowledgments, retransmissions, sequencing, and a checksum. IP (Internet Protocol) supplies addressing and routing. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)’s reliability and checksum are not confidentiality or cryptographic authentication. HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) adds TLS (Transport Layer Security) security at a different level.
questions.teach: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) handles reliable delivery. It does not itself encrypt your message or prove the other party’s identity.
questions.example: A file download needs all bytes in order. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) can retransmit missing data; TLS (Transport Layer Security) is needed separately to protect confidentiality and authenticate the server.

questions.title: Dormant program and C2
questions.q: A program or part of a program lies dormant until triggered by the C2 server. What is it?
questions.answer: Bot. A malicious bot is a program on a compromised device that receives instructions from a command-and-control (C2 (Command and Control)) server. It can wait for a command before carrying out an action. A botnet is a collection of these controlled devices. Distinguish a logic bomb: code activated by a specified condition, such as a date or file deletion. A backdoor provides concealed access.
questions.teach: C2 (Command and Control) means command and control. In this question, the remote server issuing instructions identifies the program as a bot; the collection of controlled devices is a botnet.
questions.example: A timed destructive routine is a logic bomb. An infected workstation waiting for remote instructions is a bot. Both can be dormant, but they are classified by different behavior.

questions.title: Hard fork
questions.q: What splits one blockchain instance into two through an incompatible protocol change?
questions.answer: Hard fork is the guide’s intended term. It changes consensus rules incompatibly, so nodes following different rules can maintain different chains. A persistent split depends on participants continuing both histories; a hard fork need not always leave two lasting communities. A soft fork tightens accepted rules compatibly for older nodes.
questions.teach: A protocol disagreement is different from two miners briefly finding competing blocks.
questions.example: One group adopts a rule that older nodes reject while another group continues the old rules. Their accepted transaction histories can diverge.

questions.title: Checksum
questions.q: What tool checks integrity of packet content?
questions.answer: Checksum. The receiver recomputes an error-detection value and compares it with the transmitted value to detect accidental corruption. An ordinary Internet checksum is not SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) and does not defend against an attacker who can alter data and recompute the checksum. Cryptographic integrity requires a suitable authenticated mechanism such as a MAC or signature.
questions.teach: An error check catches transmission damage. Authenticating malicious changes requires a stronger, trusted construction.
questions.example: A bit flips while a segment is transmitted and the checksum comparison fails. The receiver can discard it; reliable transport may retransmit.

questions.title: Why patching becomes easier
questions.q: How do bandwidth, cloud computing, big data/analytics, and virtualization alleviate security-update pressure?
questions.answer: More bandwidth speeds patch distribution, although deployments still need scheduling. Cloud-based and centralized management can coordinate updates across fleets, while customers retain responsibilities for their own systems and configurations. Analytics helps inventory systems, prioritize exposure, and detect failed updates. Virtualization supports representative test environments, snapshots, and rollback. Together these reduce transfer, coordination, decision, and testing costs. They do not remove compatibility testing, outages, or zero-day risk.

questions.title: Viruses and other malware
questions.q: What are the major types of computer viruses, and how do virus, worm, scareware, adware, spyware, and backdoor differ?
questions.answer: A virus attaches to a host file or document and replicates when the host runs; a worm is a standalone program that can propagate across networks. Scareware uses fraudulent alarms to pressure payment or installation. Adware displays unwanted advertising; spyware secretly collects information; a backdoor bypasses normal access controls. In this textbook’s Chapter 2, viruses include program/file viruses and macro viruses, with appender infection and armored concealment techniques: Swiss cheese, split infection, oligomorphic, polymorphic, and metamorphic mutation. Boot-sector viruses are another common category, but the supplied edition emphasizes the preceding list. The guide labels this Ch. 1; the relevant detail is actually Ch. 2, pp. 55–65.
questions.teach: Compare how malware spreads, hides, and acts. These categories can overlap: a backdoor may install spyware that includes a keylogger.
questions.example: An infected document executes a malicious macro; a network worm spreads independently; a fake antivirus page scares a user into paying. Each has a different mechanism and defense.

questions.title: Confidentiality authentication obfuscation
questions.q: How do confidentiality, authentication, and obfuscation correlate in cryptographic applications?
questions.answer: Confidentiality limits who can read data, usually through encryption. Authentication establishes a claimed identity or data origin through a suitable cryptographic protocol; a digital signature can bind a message to a signing key. Obfuscation makes information or implementation details harder to understand, and the textbook includes it among cryptographic protections. These goals complement one another but do not substitute for one another. Encryption to a recipient’s public key does not by itself identify the sender; an ordinary hash does not authenticate an origin; signing does not encrypt the message. For secrecy plus sender authentication, use a properly designed encrypted and authenticated scheme.
questions.teach: Ask three separate questions: who can read, who created or approved it, and what details are being obscured?
questions.example: A sender signs a document with the sender’s private signing key and protects the content for the recipient. The recipient decrypts and verifies using the appropriate keys and a trusted identity binding.
questions.correct: Encryption protects reading; authentication proves origin; obfuscation obscures details

A signature automatically hides the message
Obfuscation always replaces encryption

questions.title: Collision resistance
questions.q: Hash algorithms are naturally resistant to hash collisions. Why?
questions.answer: Qualify the premise: a well-designed cryptographic hash aims for computational collision resistance. A fixed n-bit digest has 2^n possible outputs, so different inputs must sometimes collide. Good output distribution and no practical structural shortcuts make finding a collision expensive. The generic birthday bound is roughly 2^(n/2) work to find any pair; finding an input for a particular digest is a different preimage problem. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) produces 256 bits (64 hexadecimal characters), with an ideal generic collision bound around 2^128. MD5 and SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm)-1 demonstrate that not every hash is collision resistant. Collision resistant never means collision impossible.
questions.teach: A large output space makes a matching pair hard to find, but fixed-length outputs cannot uniquely represent every possible input.
questions.example: Two distinct files could share a digest. A trusted expected hash can help verify a download, but an attacker changing both file and untrusted posted hash defeats that simple comparison.
questions.correct: Large well-distributed outputs make finding collisions computationally difficult
distractors: Collisions are mathematically impossible
Hashing encrypts every input uniquely
All hash algorithms have equal collision resistance

questions.title: Blockchain mechanics and tradeoffs
questions.q: How does blockchain work? What are its pros and cons?
questions.answer: Transactions are grouped into blocks. A block header commits to transaction data through a Merkle root and includes the previous block’s hash. Altering data changes its hash and breaks later commitments. Nodes validate transactions and consensus determines the accepted history. In Bitcoin, proof of work requires miners to search nonces for a header hash meeting a target; the accepted valid chain has the greatest cumulative work. More confirmations make rewriting history harder under the network’s security assumptions. Benefits include shared auditability and tamper evidence. Costs include proof-of-work energy use, throughput/latency limits, public-data privacy issues, key loss, and difficult correction of erroneous entries. Blockchain is not an absolute guarantee of truth or immutability, and not all blockchains use proof of work.
questions.teach: Hashes connect history; signatures authorize spending; consensus resolves competing histories. None does all three jobs alone.
questions.example: Change an old record in a teaching chain. Its hash and descendants no longer match. Rehashing a local copy is easy in a toy demo; convincing a real consensus network is the costly part.
questions.correct: Hash links plus validation and consensus create a shared tamper-evident history
distractors: Encryption alone makes every transaction private
A nonce is the owner’s password
Every blockchain must use Bitcoin mining

questions.title: Bitcoin and ownership transfer
questions.q: What is a bitcoin?
questions.answer: Bitcoin is a peer-to-peer digital currency whose transaction history is recorded on a blockchain. A spender authorizes use of earlier unspent transaction outputs by satisfying their spending conditions, typically with a digital signature created using the spender’s private key. A new output specifies conditions for the receiver. Nodes verify authorization and check for double spending; mining orders valid transactions through proof of work. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) contributes to hashing and proof of work, not encryption of a coin. An address is commonly derived from a key or script and is not always the raw public key. Public ledger transparency provides pseudonymity, not guaranteed anonymity. Miners receive a block subsidy and transaction fees as incentives.
questions.teach: Ownership means the ability to authorize spending under the output’s rules. You transfer spending rights through a transaction; you do not email a secret coin file.
questions.example: Alice signs a transaction spending an output she controls and creating one for Bob. Others verify it with public information. Bob later spends by satisfying his output’s conditions.
questions.correct: A peer-to-peer currency with signature-authorized spending and blockchain consensus
distractors: A coin encrypted with SHA-256 and emailed
A central-bank database with no signatures
An anonymous password shared by all miners

questions.title: CIA and risk
questions.q: Which protection matches confidentiality, integrity, and availability respectively?
questions.answer: Confidentiality restricts disclosure, integrity protects against unauthorized alteration, and availability provides access when needed. An asset has value; a vulnerability is a weakness; a threat can cause harm; risk concerns likelihood and impact. Risk responses include accept, avoid, mitigate, and transfer. Controls can be technical, administrative, or physical.
questions.teach: Confidentiality means only permitted people can see the data. Integrity means the data is not changed without permission. Availability means authorized users can get the data or service when needed.
questions.example: A hospital considers ransomware risk to patient records. Backups improve recovery, access controls restrict disclosure, and monitoring detects changes.
questions.correct: Keep information private; prevent unauthorized changes; keep services usable by authorized people.
distractors: CPU, Internet, and antivirus
Only encryption strength
The same property under three names

questions.q: How do motivations and access distinguish threat actors?
questions.answer: Organized crime often seeks profit; hacktivists pursue ideological goals; nation-state actors may seek espionage or disruption; insiders already have trusted access; script kiddies rely on existing tools; vulnerability brokers sell knowledge. questions.title: Five defense principles
questions.q: Which example correctly applies the principles of layering, limiting, diversity, obscurity, and simplicity?
questions.answer: Layering adds multiple safeguards. Limiting gives only necessary access. Diversity reduces shared failure modes across products or controls. Obscurity hides unnecessary details but cannot be the sole defense. Simplicity makes controls easier to understand and manage. Frameworks and reference architectures organize a security program; some are regulatory, industry-specific, national, or international.
questions.teach: Layering means several protective layers. Limiting means giving only necessary access. Diversity reduces reliance on one kind of protection. Obscurity hides unnecessary information but cannot replace real security. Simplicity keeps controls understandable and manageable.
questions.example: Email filtering, a standard-user account, endpoint monitoring, and recovery procedures protect different points in a phishing incident.
questions.correct: Use multiple safeguards, grant only needed access, vary protection methods, hide unnecessary details, and keep rules understandable.
distractors: Publish all secrets to simplify access
Use only one secret product
Give all users administrator rights

questions.title: Defense in depth and architecture
questions.q: How should a business use choke points, visibility, availability, and scalability when designing defenses?
questions.answer: Use safeguards at both perimeter and endpoint. A choke point is a controlled entry or exit where traffic can be inspected; internal segmentation also matters. Visibility requires useful telemetry at these boundaries and on hosts. Redundancy reduces single points of failure, while scalability supports changing workload. Balance security with business availability, budget, and capacity. The castle analogy illustrates defense in depth: a gate, walls, guards, and internal locks protect different boundaries. In a business, filtering, MFA (Multi Factor Authentication), least privilege, application allowlisting, EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), monitoring, and recovery provide complementary layers. If a phishing message passes the filter, other layers can still restrict execution, account access, lateral movement, and damage.
questions.teach: A choke point is a controlled place where traffic passes. Visibility means collecting evidence of activity. Availability means keeping services working. Scalability means handling growth. For example, a store checks traffic entering its network, keeps payment computers separate from other systems, records activity on staff devices, and provides a backup network device so one failure does not stop sales.
questions.example: A store checks traffic entering its network, separates payment computers from other computers, collects activity records from staff devices, and uses a backup device so one failure does not stop sales.
questions.correct: Inspect traffic at controlled entry points, collect useful records, provide backup paths, and plan for growing traffic.

Visibility means capturing only public web pages
Redundancy makes filtering rules unnecessary

questions.title: IDS versus IPS
questions.q: What is the difference between an Intrusion Detection System (IDS) and an Intrusion Prevention System (IPS)?
questions.answer: An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) detects suspicious activity and alerts. An IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) can actively block or disrupt traffic or activity. Either can use signatures, heuristics, behavior, or other techniques; an IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) does not require AI. Host IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) observes local activity; network controls observe traffic. Tune false positives and false negatives in light of business impact.
questions.teach: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) stands for Intrusion Detection System. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) stands for Intrusion Prevention System. Detection raises an alert. Prevention can take action to stop activity. Both need careful rules so normal work is not mistaken for an attack.
questions.example: An alert-only sensor reports suspicious traffic. An inline prevention rule blocks the same traffic, potentially interrupting legitimate service if the rule is wrong.
questions.correct: An IDS detects suspicious activity and alerts; an IPS can also block or interrupt suspicious activity.
distractors: IDS always blocks packets
IPS always requires AI
An antivirus database makes false negatives impossible

questions.title: PCAP flow proxy and allowlisting
questions.q: Which description correctly distinguishes packet capture, flow records, a proxy, and application allowlisting?
questions.answer: Full PCAP (Packet Capture) records packet bytes within capture limits, useful for detailed reconstruction; encrypted payloads remain encrypted without suitable keys. Flow records summarize conversations such as endpoints, times, ports, and byte counts. A proxy mediates application requests and can enforce policy and log activity. Application allowlisting permits approved software and restricts other execution. These controls complement rather than replace one another.
questions.teach: Packet capture records observed packet contents within recording limits. Flow records summarize who communicated, when, and how much. A proxy receives and forwards application requests while applying rules. Application allowlisting prevents unapproved programs from running. These are four different jobs.
questions.example: An analyst finds a long outbound connection in flow logs, examines available packet evidence, then correlates it with proxy and endpoint events.
questions.correct: Packet capture stores packet bytes; flow records summarize connections; a proxy handles requests; allowlisting controls which programs run.

questions.title: DDoS SYN flood and Slowloris
questions.q: How do SYN flooding and Slowloris affect availability?
questions.answer: Denial of service exhausts resources or disrupts access; distributed DoS (Denial of Service) uses multiple sources. A SYN flood abuses half-open TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection state. Slowloris holds many HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) connections with incomplete, slow requests and may work from few sources. Mitigations include upstream filtering, rate and connection limits, appropriate timeouts, SYN protections, and capacity planning. DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) can distract responders but is not always a distraction or a race condition.
questions.teach: Bandwidth floods and application connection exhaustion stress different resources. Match mitigation to the bottleneck.
questions.example: A service is unavailable despite modest bandwidth because many connections remain incomplete. Appropriate connection limits and timeouts address this pattern.
questions.correct: They consume connection resources and deny legitimate access
distractors: All DoS attacks require a giant botnet
Slowloris encrypts a database
A SYN flood is simply a race condition

questions.title: SQL injection versus XSS
questions.q: What changes when malicious input reaches a SQL query versus a browser?
questions.answer: SQL (Structured Query Language) injection makes untrusted input influence database query structure. Parameterized queries keep data separate from SQL (Structured Query Language) commands; least-privilege database accounts limit harm. XSS (Cross Site Scripting) causes attacker-controlled script to execute in a user’s browser in a trusted site’s context. Use context-aware output encoding, safe APIs, and appropriate sanitization for allowed HTML (Hypertext Markup Language). Input validation supports both but is insufficient alone. WebGoat is a deliberately vulnerable teaching application. Neither attack is limited to one operating system. A buffer overflow occurs when a program writes beyond a buffer’s allocated boundary. It can corrupt adjacent memory, crash the program, or enable code execution. Prevent it through bounds checking, memory-safe programming, and patching; DEP/NX, ASLR, and stack protections add mitigation. SQL (Structured Query Language) injection instead changes a database command through unsafe input; XSS (Cross Site Scripting) executes injected content in a victim browser. These are different interpreters and require different defenses.
questions.teach: Ask where the injected content is interpreted: database query engine or victim browser. XSS (Cross Site Scripting) is not automatically full server control.
questions.example: A search value must remain a SQL (Structured Query Language) parameter. A comment displayed on a page must remain text or sanitized allowed HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) rather than executable script.
questions.correct: SQLi changes query interpretation; XSS executes script in the browser
distractors: Both are prevented by antivirus alone
XSS always takes full control of the application server

questions.title: Social-engineering families
questions.q: How do phishing, spear phishing, smishing, vishing, and a 419 scam differ?
questions.answer: Phishing uses deceptive communication to elicit information or action. Spear phishing targets particular recipients using tailored context. Smishing uses SMS; vishing uses voice. A 419 or advance-fee scam promises a benefit to obtain money or sensitive data upfront. Scareware creates false security urgency. Verify requests through independent trusted channels and report suspicious messages.

questions.title: Metasploit and SET business case
questions.q: What do the Metasploit and SET labs demonstrate for a business?
questions.answer: Metasploit organizes authorized security testing through exploit, payload, auxiliary, and post-exploitation capabilities. SET (Social Engineer Toolkit) is a separate TrustedSec social-engineering toolkit that can integrate with Metasploit; it is not simply a Metasploit module. The credential-harvesting lab demonstrates how user trust can disclose credentials without a software exploit. Prevent with training, filtering, phishing-resistant MFA (Multi Factor Authentication), and login monitoring. If credentials are disclosed, report, reset affected secrets from a trusted device, revoke sessions, and investigate related access. MFA (Multi Factor Authentication) combines distinct factor categories: something you know, have, or are. A password plus another password is not MFA (Multi Factor Authentication). MFA (Multi Factor Authentication) is a major defense against stolen passwords; phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO (Fast IDentity Online)/WebAuthn resist deceptive-site authentication. Account monitoring, session revocation, least privilege, and endpoint security remain necessary alongside MFA (Multi Factor Authentication).
questions.teach: Explain the weakness, business consequence, evidence, and defense. Exact tool-menu commands are not the stated exam priority.
questions.example: A fake staff login collects a test password in the isolated lab. A business analogue is account takeover leading to exposed records or fraudulent actions.

questions.title: Keylogger and encryption boundaries
questions.q: Why can a keylogger steal information even when a website uses HTTPS?
questions.answer: A keylogger records input on the endpoint, often before TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts it for transport. Software variants may intercept input APIs, run with elevated privileges, or observe forms; hardware variants can sit between keyboard and computer. Not every keylogger requires process injection or admin rights. Defend with endpoint monitoring, least privilege, updates, application controls, physical inspection where appropriate, and phishing-resistant authentication. Transport encryption alone cannot secure a compromised endpoint. Phishing is an important delivery route in the lab context: a deceptive attachment or download may install a software keylogger. Other routes include compromised software, exploitation, and physical installation of hardware. A cloned login page captures submitted credentials directly and does not require a keylogger. Physical access controls address hardware capture; endpoint controls address malicious software.
questions.teach: Protection during transmission does not protect the moment data is typed on a compromised device.
questions.example: The lab’s isolated victim records test keystrokes. An organization should investigate the endpoint and account access rather than assume HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) prevented disclosure.
questions.correct: The endpoint can capture keystrokes before transport encryption

questions.title: Hardening and patch workflow
questions.q: What belongs in OS hardening and a safe patch rollout?
questions.answer: Inventory assets, apply tested updates, use standard-user accounts, remove unnecessary services, enable appropriate endpoint firewall and protection, restrict software execution, and monitor changes. A patch workflow downloads, tests, pilots, schedules, deploys, and verifies, with rollback planning. NAC (Network Access Control) checks access posture; GPO (Group Policy Object) distributes domain policy. Patching addresses known vulnerabilities but does not eliminate zero-days. Legacy tool names in notes are historical examples, not a current shopping list. Use a standard non-administrator account for routine work and elevate only for approved tasks. Maintain an asset inventory, remove unnecessary software, disable unneeded services, restrict exposed ports, configure host firewalls, keep antivirus/EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) current, and enable appropriate automatic updates. Test and stage changes where needed, verify installation, and monitor failures. An antivirus detects known or suspicious malicious content; EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) adds investigation telemetry and response capabilities.

questions.title: Visibility and incident interpretation
questions.q: How should an analyst interpret an attack timeline?
questions.answer: Correlate host process events, network connections, authentication logs, and file changes. A SOC (Security Operations Center) coordinates monitoring and response. EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) supplies endpoint detection and response evidence. Reconnaissance gathers information; privilege escalation increases rights; credential dumping extracts stored authentication material; SMB (Server Message Block) commonly supports network file sharing. Process hollowing replaces or maps malicious code into another process context. PowerShell is an administration shell and scripting environment; a sandbox is an isolated execution environment. DLL (Dynamic Link Library) means Dynamic Link Library. Infiltration gains entry; exfiltration removes information. For a business explanation, connect the sequence to impact: initial access may expose accounts; privilege escalation expands access; credential dumping can enable impersonation; process hollowing can conceal execution; C2 (Command and Control) carries remote instructions; exfiltration removes data. Correlate identity, process, file, and network evidence. The SOC (Security Operations Center) investigates and coordinates containment; EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) can expose process ancestry and support endpoint isolation. A penetration test demonstrates a weakness and its potential consequences; it does not by itself prove a real breach occurred.
questions.teach: Separate the tools, techniques, evidence, and outcomes. Seeing a tool name alone does not establish malicious intent.
questions.example: An Office process starts unusual PowerShell, followed by a new outbound connection and credential access. Build a timeline, identify affected hosts, preserve evidence, and contain according to the incident plan.
questions.correct: Correlate process, network, identity, and file evidence into a timeline
distractors: Treat all PowerShell use as proof of compromise
Sandbox means the same as PowerShell
Exfiltration means installing a software update

questions.q: What do the VirtualBox network adapters and snapshots contribute to safe testing?
questions.answer: The host runs VirtualBox and the guest operating systems. The lab uses Kali and Windows 7 guests with an internal network for guest-to-guest tests and NAT (Network Address Translation) for controlled Internet access during setup. questions.answer: Static work inspects HTML (Hypertext Markup Language), scripts, redirects, and embedded references without execution. Dynamic work observes behavior in an isolated environment, including processes, files, registry, and traffic. Reputation checks compare against previous reports. Automation is fast but can miss new threats; manual investigation provides context but takes skill and time. A legitimate site can be compromised. Firebug, Malzilla, Wepawet, JSUnpack, SiteAdvisor, and Safe Web are course-era examples.

questions.title: Hash encryption and signatures
questions.q: Which cryptographic operation should you use for secrecy, comparison, or signed origin?
questions.answer: Encryption protects content confidentiality and is reversible with the correct key. Hashing produces a deterministic fixed-length digest with no intended inverse. A signature uses a private signing key and is checked with a corresponding public key to authenticate authorized data and detect alteration. A bare hash has no secret and does not prove origin. HMAC (Hash based Message Authentication Code) combines a secret key and hash for integrity and shared-key authentication; it is not encryption and does not provide the same public verification as a signature.
questions.teach: Choose the operation by the required property rather than calling every cryptographic output ciphertext.
questions.example: A document can be hashed for comparison, signed to show approval, and encrypted for its intended reader. These operations have separate roles.
questions.correct: Encrypt for secrecy, hash for comparison, sign for verifiable authorization
distractors: Decrypt SHA-256 to recover the message
Use a bare hash to prove sender identity
Signing automatically encrypts the whole document

questions.title: Symmetric and asymmetric keys
questions.q: Which keys protect a message for Bob and allow Bob to verify Alice’s signature?
questions.answer: Symmetric encryption shares one secret for encryption and decryption and is efficient for bulk data. Public-key encryption uses the recipient’s public key and recipient’s private key to decrypt. Signing uses the sender’s private key and verification uses the sender’s public key. Verify the binding between a public key and a claimed identity. AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is symmetric; RSA (Rivest Shamir Adleman) and ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) belong to asymmetric families. DES and 3DES are historical course examples, not preferred new-system choices.
questions.teach: For confidentiality, use the recipient’s public encryption key so the recipient’s private key can decrypt. For a signature, the sender uses the sender’s private signing key; others verify with the corresponding trusted public key. The private keys remain secret.
questions.example: Alice wants only Bob to read a message and wants Bob to verify her approval. She protects it for Bob and signs it using her own signing key.
questions.correct: Encrypt for Bob using Bob’s public key; Alice signs using her private key, and Bob verifies using Alice’s trusted public key.
distractors: Encrypt with sender public key for only Bob to read
Share all private keys for authentication
Use receiver private key on the sender’s machine

questions.title: RSA arithmetic
questions.q: How does the classroom RSA example connect public and private exponents?
questions.answer: For distinct primes p and q, n=pq and φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1). Choose e with gcd(e,φ(n))=1 and choose d so ed ≡ 1 mod φ(n). Textbook notation may use m for φ(n). Classroom encryption is c=m^e mod n and decryption is m=c^d mod n. With p=5, q=11, n=55, φ=40, e=3, d=27: message 7 gives ciphertext 13 and decrypts to 7. The notes’ condition using e and n is incorrect; coprimality with φ(n) is essential. Small unpadded examples teach arithmetic and are not secure deployments.
questions.teach: The private exponent reverses the public exponent modulo n for correctly constructed RSA (Rivest Shamir Adleman). Real implementations require safe key sizes and padding.
questions.example: 3×27=81 leaves remainder 1 modulo 40. Then 7³ mod 55=13 and 13²⁷ mod 55=7.
questions.correct: Choose e coprime to φ(n), then d as its modular inverse
distractors: Choose e equal to φ(n)

questions.title: Nonce Merkle root and tampering
questions.q: What separate jobs do a proof-of-work nonce, a Merkle root, and the previous-block hash perform?
questions.answer: A proof-of-work nonce is a value miners vary while searching for a block-header hash meeting a target. A Merkle root commits to the block’s transactions using a tree of hashes. The previous-block hash links a block to its predecessor. Altering a transaction changes its commitment and invalidates later links unless recomputed. A toy rehash demonstration is not the full security model: distributed validation and cumulative proof of work make rewriting accepted history difficult.
questions.teach: A nonce is a search value. The Merkle root is computed from transaction hashes. The previous-block hash identifies the earlier block being built upon. These values support different parts of the block structure.
questions.example: Changing one transaction changes the Merkle root, then its block header hash and the descendants’ required links.
questions.correct: The nonce is varied to search for a qualifying hash; the Merkle root summarizes the transactions; the previous-block hash links to earlier history.
distractors: Nonce is the receiver’s private key

questions.title: Bitcoin incentives privacy and double spending
questions.q: Why use signatures, incentives, and consensus together in Bitcoin?
questions.answer: Signatures demonstrate authorization to spend. Nodes check spending rules, including whether an output is unspent. Consensus orders transactions so competing spends do not both become accepted history. A block subsidy and fees incentivize miners. Public records use addresses or spending scripts rather than mandatory civil identities, but linked transactions can reveal relationships. This is pseudonymity. Nakamoto’s paper contrasts verification by cryptographic proof with the reversal costs, mediation, and trust demands of financial intermediaries.
questions.teach: Authorization does not establish which of two conflicting authorized spends came first; network agreement addresses that ordering problem.
questions.example: An owner attempts to spend the same output twice. Both signatures could be valid, but both transactions cannot be accepted in one valid history.
questions.correct: Signatures authorize, consensus orders, and rewards motivate participation
distractors: Hashing alone prevents all double spending
All Bitcoin addresses guarantee anonymity
Miners can authorize spending anyone’s coins

questions.title: TCP UDP IP and handshake
questions.q: What different jobs do TCP, UDP, and IP perform when computers communicate?
questions.answer: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) provides a reliable ordered byte stream, using SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK for conventional connection establishment. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) provides datagrams without TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)-style delivery or ordering guarantees and is useful where applications tolerate loss or implement their own recovery. Both operate at the transport layer. IP (Internet Protocol) addresses and routes packets at the network layer with best-effort delivery. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is not restricted to private networks, and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) does not guarantee timeliness or encryption. Packet lengths can vary. A network packet is a unit of data handled at the network layer, not the smallest possible unit of transmission. Its header contains addressing and control fields; its payload (body) carries the data, including higher-layer headers. Bits, link-layer frames, IP (Internet Protocol) packets, and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) segments name different units. A TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) reverse shell uses TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) for the outbound shell connection; TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) reliability does not make that connection trustworthy.
questions.teach: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) puts received bytes in order and retransmits missing data when possible. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) sends individual messages called datagrams without automatically recovering missing messages or putting them in order. IP (Internet Protocol) handles addressing and forwarding packets between networks; best effort means it does not promise delivery.
questions.example: A voice application may prioritize timely delivery over retransmitting old audio; a file transfer needs all bytes. Both rely on IP (Internet Protocol) routing.
questions.correct: TCP delivers an ordered byte stream with recovery; UDP sends separate messages without those guarantees; IP forwards packets toward destinations.
distractors: IP guarantees every byte in order
UDP is only allowed on private networks
TCP stands for Transportation Control Protocol

questions.title: Network administration protocols
questions.q: Which statement correctly matches DNS, SNMP, ICMP, FTP, SMTP, and POP to their jobs?
questions.answer: DNS (Domain Name System) resolves names and other records; poisoning supplies false resolution information. DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) authenticates signed DNS (Domain Name System) data and integrity when correctly validated, without encrypting ordinary DNS (Domain Name System) queries. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) monitors and manages devices; v3 supports stronger protection. ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) carries network control and diagnostic messages, including ping. Traditional FTP (File Transfer Protocol) transfers files without encryption: port 21 controls, port 20 is traditionally active-mode data, while passive mode negotiates data ports. SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) transfers mail and POP (Post Office Protocol) retrieves it. Wireshark analyzes packets; log correlation helps investigation.
questions.teach: Each protocol defines rules for a different communication task. DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) adds authentication of signed DNS (Domain Name System) data, not encryption of ordinary queries. Traditional FTP (File Transfer Protocol) does not encrypt its transfers. A protocol’s name alone does not mean its traffic is confidential.
questions.example: A name resolves unexpectedly, so an analyst checks DNS (Domain Name System) evidence and validation. Separate authentication logs and packet metadata help establish the incident timeline.
questions.correct: DNS looks up names; SNMP manages devices; ICMP carries network diagnostic/control messages; FTP transfers files; SMTP sends mail; POP retrieves mail.

FTP always uses port 20 for all traffic
ICMP is a mail retrieval service

questions.title: Chapter 3 overview and study route
questions.q: Which Chapter 3 protection best addresses a lost, powered-off laptop containing confidential files?
questions.answer: Steganography hides the existence of data; encryption hides readable content. ROT13 is a substitution cipher, and XOR gives 0 for equal input bits and 1 for different bits. Stream ciphers process streams; block ciphers process fixed-size blocks. Diffusion spreads a plaintext change through the output; confusion obscures the relation between key and ciphertext. Secure randomness and key management matter. Diffie-Hellman establishes a shared secret; ephemeral exchanges can support forward secrecy when used correctly. Downgrade attacks force weaker options. TPM (Trusted Platform Module) and HSM (Hardware Security Module) protect cryptographic operations and keys; full-disk encryption protects stored data. Resource, power, and latency constraints influence implementation choices.
questions.teach: Full-disk encryption protects data saved on the drive. It does not prevent every attack after the device is unlocked. Other Chapter 3 concepts have separate definition questions, including steganography, forward secrecy, TPM (Trusted Platform Module), HSM (Hardware Security Module), and stream and block ciphers.

questions.title: Why attacks succeed
questions.q: How do vulnerable software, configuration, resource limits, and business processes create different weaknesses?
questions.teach: A flaw can exist in the product, in its settings, in its limited capacity, or in the way people do business. Fixing one category does not automatically fix another.
questions.answer: Chapter 1 groups weaknesses into widespread vulnerabilities, configuration issues, poor software design, hardware limitations, and enterprise issues. Unsupported or end-of-life products may lack patches. Default settings and excessive account privileges are configuration issues. Unsafe input, error handling, and races are design issues. Resource exhaustion consumes CPU (Central Processing Unit), memory, storage, or connections. Business-process compromise manipulates legitimate workflows; undocumented assets create system sprawl. Defenses include inventory, supported software, hardened settings, safe design, capacity controls, and verification of unusual business requests.
questions.example: A patched accounting system still processes a fraudulent payment because staff skip the callback check. This is a process weakness even though the software is up to date.
questions.correct: Different weakness categories require different controls
distractors: Patching fixes every process weakness
All successful attacks require a zero-day
More bandwidth fixes excessive user privileges

questions.title: Asset threat vulnerability and vector
questions.q: How do an asset, a vulnerability, a threat, and risk relate in a security decision?
questions.teach: An asset is something valuable. A vulnerability is a weakness. A threat is a potential cause of harm. Risk considers how likely harm is and how serious it would be. An attack vector is the route used to reach the target.
questions.answer: An asset is something valuable. A threat is potential harm; a threat actor can cause that harm. A vulnerability is a weakness. An attack vector is a route or means of attack; the attack surface includes the collection of exposed opportunities. Risk concerns potential loss in context, including likelihood and impact. A threat is not proof an incident occurred. Reducing unnecessary services can shrink attack surface, while fixing a flaw removes a particular vulnerability.

questions.correct: A valuable resource has a weakness; something could exploit it; risk considers the likelihood and impact of the resulting harm.
distractors: Asset and threat always mean the same thing

Every threat is already a successful breach

questions.title: Risk response choices
questions.q: A business installs a patch to reduce a known security risk. Which risk response is it using?
questions.teach: Mitigate means reduce. A patch repairs a weakness, reducing the chance of a successful attack. Acceptance means knowingly living with risk; avoidance means stopping the risky activity; transfer shifts some consequences, such as through insurance.
questions.answer: Accepting risk acknowledges exposure under a deliberate decision. Avoidance stops the risky activity. Transfer shifts some financial consequences through insurance or an appropriate agreement; it does not remove all responsibility. Mitigation reduces likelihood or impact through controls. Deterrence discourages attackers. A course expression such as threat × vulnerability × cost is a conceptual aid, not a measured probability formula unless its variables are defined.
questions.example: For a risky remote service, canceling it is avoidance; adding MFA (Multi Factor Authentication) is mitigation; buying suitable insurance transfers some loss; documenting a tolerable residual exposure is acceptance.
questions.correct: Mitigation: reducing the likelihood or impact of harm.
distractors: Buying insurance patches software
Accept means the risk was eliminated
Mitigate means never using the service
questions.goal: Explain Risk response choices in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Buying insurance patches software

questions.title: People products and procedures
questions.q: Why can a security product fail without people and procedures?
questions.teach: A tool needs someone to configure and use it, and a repeatable procedure for acting on what it finds.
questions.answer: The textbook’s layers are products, people, and policies/procedures. Products include technical and physical safeguards. People configure and use them. Procedures define approved actions and escalation. Technical controls use technology, administrative controls guide behavior, and physical controls restrict physical access. Security must support useful business work; inconvenient controls may cause workarounds. Compliance is one requirement, not proof that attacks cannot succeed.
questions.example: A sensor produces alerts, but no one owns the review queue. Buying another sensor does not solve the missing monitoring responsibility.
questions.correct: Tools, responsible people, and defined procedures must work together
distractors: A product automatically creates an incident process
Only IT staff affect security
Every compliant system is immune to attack

questions.title: Threat actor attributes
questions.q: Which facts help assess what a threat actor can do and why they might do it?
questions.teach: Capability means skills and tools. Resources include money and time. Access describes what the actor can already reach. Motivation is the reason for acting. A trusted employee and an outside criminal may have different opportunities even when both want money.
questions.answer: Compare sophistication, funding/resources, internal versus external position, and intent. Script kiddies use existing tools; hacktivists pursue ideological goals; criminals pursue gain; competitors may steal valuable research; brokers sell vulnerability knowledge; nation-state actors may conduct sustained espionage. APT (Advanced Persistent Threat) describes sustained targeted activity, often associated with state actors. Insiders include employees, contractors, and partners. Assess behaviors and evidence rather than assuming nationality or a single label proves intent.
questions.example: An insider can export customer records through ordinary access, while a well-funded external group can patiently target a specific research system.
questions.correct: Their skills, money and tools, existing access, and motivation.
distractors: All insiders have malicious intent
Only experts can use attack tools
A zero-day is a category of employee

questions.title: Roles and fundamental principles
questions.q: Which pairing correctly matches a security role with its duties?
questions.teach: In this textbook, the security administrator analyzes and designs solutions for users. A technician installs, configures, and troubleshoots tools. A manager supervises personnel. Layering, limiting, diversity, obscurity, and simplicity are separate principles, each with its own definition question.
questions.answer: In this textbook the CISO (Chief Information Security Officer) leads security, the manager supervises staff, the administrator manages daily technology and analyzes/designs solutions, and the technician configures and troubleshoots. Layering adds barriers; limiting grants necessary rights; diversity reduces common failure modes; obscurity conceals unnecessary details; simplicity keeps defenses manageable. Vendor diversity alone does not guarantee independence, and secrecy alone does not establish security.
questions.example: An administrator chooses a combination of access rules and endpoint controls. A technician installs and troubleshoots them. A manager allocates staffing for monitoring.
questions.correct: An administrator designs solutions and identifies users’ needs; a technician configures tools; a manager supervises the team.
distractors: A technician and CISO always have identical duties
Using two identical rules guarantees diversity
Complexity always improves security

questions.title: Data at rest in transit and in use
questions.q: Which example correctly matches data at rest, in transit, and in use?
questions.teach: Different stages expose data in different places. Storage encryption protects stored data. Protected communication helps while it travels. Permissions and endpoint protection help when programs use readable data.
questions.answer: Data at rest is stored, such as a powered-off laptop’s files. Data in transit travels across a network. Data in use is being processed on an endpoint. Disk encryption helps against offline access; TLS (Transport Layer Security) protects a connection; endpoint controls and careful access restrictions protect use. Keys, recovery, trusted devices, and authentication matter in all cases. A keylogger exposes why encrypted transport cannot rescue plaintext already captured on the endpoint.
questions.example: A payroll file on disk, the same file being uploaded, and its contents open in a running application illustrate the three states.

questions.title: Substitution ROT13 and XOR
questions.q: What do the simple ciphers teach, and what are their limits?
questions.teach: A substitution replaces symbols. ROT13 shifts letters by 13 positions. XOR compares bits: same gives 0 and different gives 1.
questions.answer: ROT13 applied twice recovers the original letters, demonstrating reversibility. XOR has the useful identity (message XOR key) XOR key = message. For example 1010 XOR 0110 = 1100, then 1100 XOR 0110 = 1010. These operations teach algorithms and keys. ROT13 has no meaningful secrecy against someone who knows the rule; repeating a short XOR key is not a secure replacement for a designed cryptographic scheme.
questions.example: Using the same XOR bit pattern twice cancels it. This is different from hashing, where there is no corresponding decryption step.
questions.correct: XOR returns 0 for equal bits and 1 for different bits
distractors: 1 XOR 1 equals 2
ROT13 is a one-way hash
XOR always gives 1

questions.title: Randomness confusion and diffusion
questions.q: Why do cryptographic randomness, confusion, and diffusion matter?
questions.teach: A secret key must be hard to predict. The output should not expose simple patterns linking the message and key.
questions.answer: Cryptographic randomness supplies unpredictable secrets. A PRNG is algorithmic and deterministic; a cryptographically secure generator must be designed and seeded appropriately. Diffusion spreads a plaintext change through output. Confusion complicates the relation between key and ciphertext. These frustrate pattern analysis, but do not excuse weak keys, implementation errors, or exposed secrets. An ordinary predictable random-number generator is not suitable simply because its output looks irregular.
questions.example: If every key is derived from the current minute, a strong cipher may still be easy to guess. Strong mathematics cannot compensate for predictable key generation.
questions.correct: Unpredictable secrets and hidden input/key patterns resist analysis
distractors: A hidden algorithm removes the need for keys
More randomness changes hash output length
Diffusion means packets arrive faster
questions.goal: Explain Randomness confusion and diffusion in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A hidden algorithm removes the need for keys

questions.title: Stream block sponge and one-time pad
questions.q: How do a stream cipher, a block cipher, a sponge construction, and a one-time pad differ?
questions.teach: These are the four constructions in this question. A stream cipher processes data using a key-dependent stream. A block cipher operates on fixed-size blocks. A sponge absorbs input and squeezes output. A true one-time pad uses a random secret key as long as the message and never reuses it.
questions.answer: A stream cipher combines data with a keystream; a block cipher transforms fixed-size blocks under a key. Secure modes determine how blocks form a message. Sponge constructions absorb input and generate output; SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm)-3 uses this family of designs, while extendable-output variants can request different lengths. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) itself has a fixed-length digest. A true one-time pad requires a uniformly random secret key as long as the message, used once only. Reusing it destroys its special security. Stream ciphers are not inherently weaker than block ciphers.
questions.example: A short password repeated across a long file is not a one-time pad even if the program uses XOR.
questions.correct: Stream ciphers process a stream; block ciphers transform fixed-size blocks; sponge designs absorb then squeeze; a one-time pad needs a truly random key used once.
distractors: All stream ciphers are always insecure
SHA-256 produces any length requested
Any repeated password is a one-time pad
questions.goal: Explain Stream block sponge and one-time pad in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: All stream ciphers are always insecure
questions.originalPrompt: How do processing structure and key use distinguish these constructions?

questions.title: Hashes HMAC and trusted comparisons
questions.q: What can a hash comparison establish, and what does HMAC add?
questions.teach: A plain hash is a fingerprint anyone can calculate. HMAC (Hash based Message Authentication Code) adds a secret shared by the parties, so unauthorized changes are harder to forge.
questions.answer: MD5, SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm) families, and RIPEMD are hash families. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) outputs 256 bits, shown by 64 hexadecimal characters. MD5 and SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm)-1 have broken collision resistance. HMAC (Hash based Message Authentication Code) uses a hash and a secret key for message authentication/integrity; it does not encrypt. Both holders of a shared HMAC (Hash based Message Authentication Code) key can produce a tag, so it is not a publicly verifiable proof of which holder acted. For download checking, the expected digest must come through a trusted channel. An attacker replacing a file and its untrusted posted hash defeats simple comparison.
questions.example: An analyst checks a downloaded file against an independently authenticated expected digest. A plain hash copied from the attacker’s page would not give the same assurance.
questions.correct: A trusted digest detects changes; HMAC adds shared-secret authentication
distractors: HMAC encrypts and hides the whole message
An untrusted posted hash proves authenticity
MD5 has guaranteed unique outputs
questions.goal: Explain Hashes HMAC (Hash based Message Authentication Code) and trusted comparisons in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: HMAC encrypts and hides the whole message

questions.title: Symmetric algorithm recognition
questions.q: Which categories contain DES, 3DES, AES, RC4, Blowfish, Twofish, and IDEA?
questions.teach: Block ciphers transform fixed-size blocks. Stream ciphers process a key-dependent stream. AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) uses 128-bit blocks with 128-, 192-, or 256-bit keys. Recognizing a historical algorithm for the exam does not make it suitable for current use.
questions.answer: DES is a symmetric block cipher with a 56-bit key. 3DES applies the DES primitive three times; the two are historical course examples. AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is a symmetric block cipher with 128-bit blocks and keys of 128, 192, or 256 bits. AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) total rounds are 10, 12, and 14 respectively; the textbook’s 9/11/13 count refers to its repeated middle-stage description, not the total standard rounds. RC4 is a historical stream cipher. Blowfish and Twofish are block ciphers; IDEA is also symmetric. Recognition is the study goal, not deploying every algorithm named in an old book.
questions.example: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard)-256 uses a 256-bit key but still transforms 128-bit blocks. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) instead names a 256-bit hash digest.
questions.correct: DES, 3DES, AES, Blowfish, Twofish, and IDEA are symmetric block ciphers; RC4 is a symmetric stream cipher.
distractors: AES-256 always uses 256-bit blocks
RSA is a symmetric stream cipher
SHA-256 is AES with a different key
questions.goal: Explain Symmetric algorithm recognition in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: AES-256 always uses 256-bit blocks

questions.title: Key distribution and hybrid encryption
questions.q: Why do secure communication systems often combine asymmetric and symmetric cryptography?
questions.teach: Asymmetric methods use a public/private key pair. Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret. Combining them avoids using expensive public-key operations for every byte of a large transfer. The parties must also authenticate the exchange.
questions.answer: In hybrid encryption, a fresh symmetric session key protects bulk data. A suitable public-key scheme protects that session key for the recipient, or an authenticated key agreement establishes it. The receiver uses the appropriate private-key capability to recover or derive the session secret, then decrypts the bulk data. PGP is the textbook example. Public keys still need trusted identity binding. The sender’s private key is not sent to the receiver, and public-key encryption alone does not authenticate who sent the message.
questions.example: A file is encrypted under a random session key. Only the intended recipient can recover that key from the protected key material and open the file.
questions.correct: Public-key techniques help establish or protect a shared secret; symmetric encryption efficiently protects the message data.
distractors: Send the recipient your private key
Encrypt every byte with an untrusted posted public key
Hash the file and call it encrypted
questions.goal: Explain Key distribution and hybrid encryption in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Send the recipient your private key
questions.originalPrompt: Why combine symmetric and asymmetric cryptography?

questions.title: RSA ECC signatures and key exchange
questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes RSA, ECC, digital signatures, and Diffie-Hellman?
questions.teach: RSA (Rivest Shamir Adleman) and ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) are mathematical foundations for particular schemes. Signatures let a recipient verify that the trusted signing key authorized specific content. Diffie-Hellman helps establish shared key material, but the exchange also needs authentication against impersonation.
questions.answer: RSA (Rivest Shamir Adleman) uses arithmetic related to large primes and supports suitable encryption/signature schemes. ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) is a family using elliptic-curve mathematics and can support signatures or agreement with different constructions. DSA is a signature algorithm, not bulk-data encryption. Diffie-Hellman establishes a shared secret; it does not by itself authenticate who participated. Ephemeral DH/ECDH can support forward secrecy so later long-term key compromise does not reveal properly established past sessions. Do not infer that every use of DH is static or every public-key algorithm has forward secrecy.
questions.example: A secure protocol authenticates the parties and establishes a fresh session secret, then uses efficient symmetric encryption for the conversation.
questions.correct: RSA and ECC support public-key constructions; signatures verify signed messages; Diffie-Hellman establishes a shared secret.
distractors: Diffie-Hellman alone proves civil identity
DSA is a disk-encryption mode
All RSA use automatically provides forward secrecy
questions.goal: Explain RSA (Rivest Shamir Adleman) ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) signatures and key exchange in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.

questions.title: Signature verification from start to finish
questions.q: What does a recipient actually check when verifying a signed message?
questions.teach: The signature must match both the message and the trusted sender key. Verifying a signature is different from decrypting a message for privacy.
questions.answer: The sender signs a representation of the message using a private signing key. The recipient verifies the signature with a trusted corresponding public key and the received message. Alteration makes verification fail under the scheme’s assumptions. Signatures support origin authentication, integrity, and evidence of authorization/non-repudiation, subject to key custody and identity trust. A valid signature proves a key authorized the signed content; it does not automatically prove the content is true or secret. The textbook’s encrypted-digest diagram is a teaching model, not a universal implementation of every signature algorithm.
questions.example: Alice signs an invoice. If an attacker changes the amount, Bob’s verification fails. If Bob instead trusts an attacker’s substitute public key, he has not authenticated Alice.
questions.correct: Verify the received message and signature using the trusted sender public key
distractors: Decrypt the message with the sender public key to guarantee secrecy
Compare two untrusted plain hashes only
Use the recipient private key to identify the sender
questions.goal: Explain Signature verification from start to finish in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.

questions.title: Attacks on cryptography
questions.q: Which example distinguishes a downgrade attack from a weak algorithm or an implementation flaw?
questions.teach: An attacker can exploit the selected protocol, the mathematical protection, or the code that implements it. These are different problems: choosing a good algorithm does not automatically make flawed software safe.
questions.answer: Ciphertext-only analysis looks for useful patterns without the plaintext. A downgrade pushes a protocol into weaker settings. Deprecated algorithms have known weaknesses or no longer provide an adequate margin. Misconfiguration or implementation mistakes can expose keys, misuse randomness, or apply a primitive incorrectly. Collision attacks seek two matching-digest inputs; preimage attacks seek input for a particular digest. The birthday bound for an ideal n-bit digest is roughly 2^(n/2), distinct from a roughly 2^n generic preimage search.
questions.example: A strong encryption algorithm does not help if its key is bundled in a public file. That failure concerns key handling rather than breaking the cipher mathematically.
questions.correct: A downgrade forces a weaker option; a weak algorithm has inadequate protection; an implementation flaw is a mistake in the program using it.
distractors: Every cryptographic incident means AES was mathematically broken
A downgrade always improves protection

questions.title: File encryption full-disk encryption and hardware
questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes file encryption, full-disk encryption, TPM, and HSM?
questions.teach: Choose the protection according to where exposure occurs. A lost locked drive differs from a program reading an unlocked document. A protected key component does not make every application immune to attack.
questions.answer: File encryption protects selected files or folders. Full-disk or volume encryption protects stored contents against offline access when keys are unavailable. A self-encrypting drive performs encryption in its controller. A TPM (Trusted Platform Module) supports platform-bound key protection and measured-state uses; it is not simply a chip that encrypts all files or always refuses every altered boot. An HSM (Hardware Security Module) is a dedicated cryptographic key/operation boundary often serving applications or multiple systems. Hardware and firmware still require trustworthy implementation, configuration, and access controls. Recovery keys and backups are necessary operational considerations.
questions.example: A company may use disk encryption for lost laptops and an HSM (Hardware Security Module) for server signing keys. Neither prevents all misuse by an already authenticated running application.
questions.correct: File encryption protects selected files; disk encryption protects stored drive data; TPM and HSM protect particular keys and cryptographic operations.
distractors: A TPM automatically encrypts every network packet
Hardware encryption has no possible vulnerabilities
File encryption always protects every temporary file on the disk

questions.title: Detection tuning and business cost
questions.q: A legitimate nightly backup repeatedly causes attack alerts. How should the security team adjust detection?
questions.teach: Tune detection means adjust the rules using investigated evidence. First confirm why the backup triggered the alert. Then reduce that harmless alert without disabling useful attack detection. Consider business impact: needless blocking interrupts work, but hiding genuine attacks leaves the organization exposed.
questions.answer: A detection signature may be a byte pattern, behavior rule, hash, or other feature; it is not always one unique hexadecimal string embedded in the file. Anomaly detection may notice new behavior but can flag unusual legitimate work. A false positive can overload analysts or interrupt service when prevention acts; a false negative can let an attack continue. Tuning uses representative traffic and investigation feedback. Redundancy, scalability, and business needs constrain inspection design.
questions.example: A large legitimate backup suddenly triggers an anomaly rule. The team investigates and adjusts the rule without disabling monitoring for all other traffic.
questions.correct: Investigate the backup, adjust the relevant rule carefully, and verify that actual attacks still generate alerts.
distractors: Every anomaly is malicious
Every signature is guaranteed unique
A zero alert rate proves perfect security

questions.title: Defacement and advance-fee scams
questions.q: How do changing a website and a 419 scam differ in mechanism and business harm?
questions.teach: Defacement changes what a site displays. An advance-fee scam persuades a person to give money or information for a promised reward.
questions.answer: A site defacement may exploit a software weakness or stolen administrative credentials to alter public content, creating reputational and integrity harm.
