questions.title: Manual automated static and dynamic
questions.q: How do manual analysis, automated analysis, static analysis, and dynamic analysis differ?
questions.teach: These are the four labels. Manual versus automated describes who performs the analysis. Static versus dynamic describes whether the program being examined runs. A person can read code manually and statically; a tool can automatically observe it running dynamically.
questions.answer: A person can read source statically or debug running code dynamically. A tool can automate either approach. Lecture 6 names Firebug and Malzilla for manual review and JSUnpack, Wepawet, and reputation services under automated tools. Inspect source for suspicious redirects, embedded frames, scripts, form handling, and external references. Legitimate pages can contain those features too, so context and behavior matter. JSUnpack is the sample answer. It unpacks JavaScript and can emulate execution; automated tools can combine static and dynamic techniques.
questions.example: A script automatically scans source without executing it: automated/static. A human watches an isolated program’s network changes: manual/dynamic.
questions.correct: Manual means a person does the work; automated means software does it; static avoids execution; dynamic observes execution.
distractors: All automated analysis is static
All manual analysis executes code
Every iframe proves malware

questions.title: Merkle proofs and hash links
questions.q: How does a Merkle proof differ from a link to the previous block?
questions.teach: One commitment summarizes transactions inside a block. Another connects that block to earlier history.
questions.answer: A Merkle tree combines transaction hashes into a root. A membership proof supplies enough sibling hashes to recompute the trusted root without downloading every transaction. It shows inclusion under that root, not that a real-world claim is true or a spend valid. A previous-block hash commits to the preceding header. Non-membership proofs require appropriate ordered/authenticated structures; not every ordinary Merkle tree automatically proves absence. Changing data affects its commitment and descendant links.
questions.example: A lightweight client can verify inclusion using a transaction and its proof path, but still needs an appropriately trusted chain/header view and validation assumptions.
questions.correct: Merkle proofs show inclusion under a root; prior hashes link block history
distractors: A Merkle proof reveals every owner’s private key
Membership proves every business claim is true
Any unsorted tree automatically proves absence

questions.title: Consensus double spending and forks
questions.q: Why can two validly signed Bitcoin transactions still conflict by trying to spend the same funds?
questions.teach: Double spending means trying to use the same digital funds twice. A person controlling a key can sign two conflicting transactions. A valid signature shows authorization, not that the funds remain unspent. Nodes check unspent outputs and agree on a valid history.
questions.answer: Nodes independently validate transactions and blocks. Bitcoin’s proof-of-work chain selection follows greatest cumulative work among valid chains; the lecture’s longest-chain phrase is a simplification. The Byzantine-generals theme concerns agreement despite faulty or malicious participants. Confirmations reduce reorganization risk under the security assumptions. A hard fork changes rules incompatibly; a soft fork restricts accepted rules compatibly for older nodes. Neither term simply means every competing branch survives or disappears by natural selection.
questions.example: Two transactions spend the same previous output and both have genuine owner signatures. They cannot both enter the same valid transaction history.
questions.correct: A signature authorizes a spend; validation and consensus must also prevent the same output from being spent twice.
distractors: A valid signature makes every conflicting spend acceptable
Any chain with more block count is always valid
Every hard fork guarantees two permanent chains

questions.title: Packets encapsulation and headers
questions.q: What is the usual nesting of an application message inside TCP/IP communication?
questions.teach: Each layer adds its own control information. The IP (Internet Protocol) payload can include a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) header and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) data. The frame carries the IP (Internet Protocol) packet across a particular local link.
questions.answer: Application data can be carried in a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) segment with ports, sequence/acknowledgment fields, and a checksum. IP (Internet Protocol) wraps transport data with addresses and routing-related header fields. A link-layer frame carries the IP (Internet Protocol) packet on a particular link. Packet lengths vary within protocol/link constraints. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is transport/OSI layer 4; IP (Internet Protocol) is network/OSI layer 3. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) does not choose the Internet route or provide encryption. Checksum error detection is distinct from authenticated integrity.
questions.example: A short message gains TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and IP (Internet Protocol) headers before link transmission. A capture can show ports and addresses even when higher-level contents are encrypted.
questions.correct: Application data is carried in a TCP segment, which is carried in an IP packet, which is carried in a link-layer frame.
distractors: TCP contains the entire Internet routing table
Every IP packet has the same fixed size
IP automatically encrypts the payload

questions.title: Firewall types and return-traffic assumptions
questions.q: How do packet-filtering firewalls, connection-aware controls, and application gateways inspect different information?
questions.teach: Different controls can see and enforce different things. Allowing a port does not prove the carried activity is safe. Proxy inspection and connection tracking also depend on their configured rules and visibility.
questions.answer: The lecture diagram associates packet filtering with network-level checks, circuit gateways with connection/session establishment, application gateways with higher-level mediation, and MAC-layer controls with link identifiers. Modern products may combine capabilities. Stateful filtering tracks connection context; a simplistic rule allowing anything resembling return traffic can be misleading. A proxy may authenticate users and restrict requests, but its visibility and policies determine effectiveness. Compare business goals and inspectable evidence rather than assuming one name guarantees protection.

questions.title: Secure protocol choices
questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes FTPS, SFTP, HTTPS, S/MIME, SRTP, and NTP?
questions.teach: Start with the application task, then identify its protection. FTPS (File Transfer Protocol over Transport Layer Security) and SFTP (Secure Shell File Transfer Protocol) use different protocols. Ordinary NTP (Network Time Protocol) does not automatically provide cryptographic protection. A secure-looking name is not a substitute for checking how the service is actually configured.
questions.answer: Traditional FTP (File Transfer Protocol) uses separate control/data connections without encryption. FTPS (File Transfer Protocol over Transport Layer Security) adds TLS (Transport Layer Security) to FTP (File Transfer Protocol); require the intended protection for control and data rather than assuming both are protected. SFTP (Secure Shell File Transfer Protocol) is file transfer over SSH (Secure Shell), not FTP (File Transfer Protocol) with a secure label. HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) protects HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) with TLS (Transport Layer Security). S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) supports email content signing/encryption, subject to key and client support. SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) protects real-time media. NTP (Network Time Protocol) synchronizes time; plain NTP (Network Time Protocol) alone is not a cryptographic guarantee (NTS (Network Time Security) is a separate security mechanism). DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) authenticates DNS (Domain Name System) data and does not encrypt ordinary queries. These clarify the lecture’s simplified secure-protocol table.
questions.example: A company moving files chooses SFTP (Secure Shell File Transfer Protocol) over SSH (Secure Shell). A signed email may remain signed beyond one transport connection, unlike merely protecting its delivery link with TLS (Transport Layer Security).
questions.correct: FTPS protects FTP with TLS; SFTP transfers files over SSH; HTTPS protects web traffic; S/MIME protects email content; SRTP protects media; NTP synchronizes clocks.

DNSSEC encrypts every web connection

questions.q: What distinct information do DNS, SNMP, and ICMP provide to a network administrator?
questions.teach: A DNS (Domain Name System) lookup investigates name resolution. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) can report managed device status. ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) messages help diagnose reachability or delivery problems. Each gives only part of the evidence; none proves every application is working correctly.
questions.answer: DNS (Domain Name System) provides hierarchical distributed name records. Poisoning can redirect resolution; validated DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) checks signed DNS (Domain Name System) data. Restricting unintended zone transfer reduces information exposure. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) agents expose permitted management information; versions 1/2c use community strings, while v3 supports stronger authentication/privacy depending on configuration. ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) echo can test reachability and latency, but a blocked response does not prove the host is down. A successful ping does not prove that an application works.
questions.example: A device answers ping but its web application fails. The network evidence establishes only part of the service path, so application logs and connection tests are needed.
questions.correct: DNS provides name records; SNMP provides device-management information; ICMP provides network-control and diagnostic messages.
distractors: A successful ping proves every application is healthy
SNMP community strings always encrypt traffic
DNSSEC makes all returned websites trustworthy

questions.title: Port mirrors taps and sensor placement
questions.q: Why might a network sensor miss an attack occurring elsewhere in the organization?
questions.teach: A switch mirror copies selected traffic and a tap observes a link. Neither automatically sees every device everywhere. Combine network observations with endpoint and account records where necessary.
questions.answer: A switch mirror copies selected port traffic to a monitoring port. A network tap provides a traffic copy from a link. Both have operational limitations; traffic may be dropped, selected incompletely, or remain encrypted. Sensors detect, collectors gather, filters enforce, and correlation engines combine evidence. Placement should cover relevant boundaries, internal movement, and business assets; simply choosing the busiest link can miss a smaller critical segment. TLS (Transport Layer Security) termination changes which content may be visible.
questions.example: A gateway sensor sees Internet traffic but not two servers talking locally on another switch. An internal mirror or other telemetry may be needed.
questions.correct: The sensor sees only traffic that actually reaches its monitored link or copied traffic feed.
distractors: The busiest link reveals every network action
Mirroring automatically decrypts TLS
A collector always blocks malware inline

questions.pitfall: The busiest link reveals every network action

questions.title: Logs correlation and retention
questions.q: How should an investigator use login, process, network, and file logs together?
questions.teach: Each record shows only part of the story. Matching related records helps identify what happened and which systems are affected. Missing logs or inconsistent clocks limit the conclusions.
questions.answer: Access logs show resource requests, audit logs record accountable actions, event logs record system/application events, and security logs describe security-related observations. Exact fields vary. Correlate identity, host, and network events using reliable time and context. Watch rejected traffic, unusual outbound connections, unsuccessful logins, and unexpected file changes. Centralized analysis helps handle volume and format differences, but collection gaps, clock differences, retention limits, and tampering affect conclusions. File-integrity monitoring detects changes; an alert still needs interpretation.
questions.example: An unusual login precedes a new process and outbound transfer. Together these support a stronger timeline than any one record alone.
questions.correct: Compare their times and event details to reconstruct activity, while checking missing records, clock differences, and how long evidence was kept.
distractors: One log contains every action forever
No retained event proves nothing happened
All file changes are definitely malicious

questions.title: Hypervisors containers and virtual desktops
questions.q: How do Type I hypervisors, Type II hypervisors, containers, and VDI differ?
questions.teach: A hypervisor manages virtual machines. A container usually shares the host kernel rather than having the same boundary as a complete guest OS (Operating System). VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure) describes delivery of desktops. VM (Virtual Machine) sprawl means uncontrolled growth that makes inventory and patching difficult.
questions.answer: Type I hypervisors run directly on hardware; Type II hypervisors run above a host OS (Operating System), as in the VirtualBox lab. Containers package applications and dependencies while sharing a kernel, with different isolation boundaries from VMs. VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure) hosts user desktops on servers. Snapshots and live migration support operations but do not automatically remove downtime or replace backups. VM (Virtual Machine) escape is a possible isolation failure; VM (Virtual Machine) sprawl is unmanaged growth. Protect the hypervisor, guests, management plane, and virtual networks. Virtual Distributed Ethernet (VDE) describes a virtual Ethernet network connecting virtual and/or physical systems; it is a networking concept, distinct from VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure)’s remotely hosted desktops.
questions.example: An organization creates twenty test VMs and forgets half of them. Those systems still need ownership, updates, and monitoring.
questions.correct: Type I runs on hardware; Type II runs on a host OS; containers commonly share a kernel; VDI provides remotely accessed desktops.
distractors: Every container has its own full guest kernel
A snapshot is an independent backup by definition
VMs never need security updates
questions.goal: Explain Hypervisors containers and virtual desktops in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Every container has its own full guest kernel

questions.title: Cloud models and responsibility
questions.q: How do SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS change what the customer manages?
questions.teach: The service arrangement determines which duties belong to the provider or customer. Accounts, data, access choices, and configuration still require attention. Public, private, community, and hybrid describe deployment arrangements rather than these service layers.
questions.answer: SaaS (Software as a Service) supplies an application; PaaS (Platform as a Service) supplies a managed platform for customer applications; IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) supplies infrastructure where customers manage their OS (Operating System)/applications. SECaaS delivers security services. Public/private/community/hybrid describe deployment arrangements, not the same categories as service models. Protect identities, configurations, data, transmission, tenant isolation, and availability according to responsibility. A CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker) helps extend enterprise policy to cloud usage. Distributed processing does not by itself mean every participant has equal authority. A public cloud offers provider services to customers generally; a private cloud is dedicated to one organization; a community cloud serves organizations with shared needs; a hybrid combines distinct cloud arrangements with integration. These describe deployment, while SaaS (Software as a Service)/PaaS (Platform as a Service)/IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) describe which service layers are supplied.
questions.example: An IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) customer still patches its own guest OS (Operating System). A SaaS (Software as a Service) customer may not patch the vendor’s servers but still controls its own user access and data-sharing choices.
questions.correct: SaaS supplies an application; PaaS supplies an application platform; IaaS supplies infrastructure while the customer manages guest operating systems and applications.
distractors: Cloud always means the provider patches every customer OS
Private cloud means there is no network
SaaS and hybrid are the same kind of category

checks.q: Two distinct files could share a digest. A trusted expected hash can help verify a download, but an attacker changing both file and untrusted posted hash defeats that simple comparison. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Large well-distributed outputs make finding collisions computationally difficult
distractors: Collisions are mathematically impossible
Hashing encrypts every input uniquely
All hash algorithms have equal collision resistance
checks.teach: A large output space makes a matching pair hard to find, but fixed-length outputs cannot uniquely represent every possible input.
checks.answer: Qualify the premise: a well-designed cryptographic hash aims for computational collision resistance. A fixed n-bit digest has 2^n possible outputs, so different inputs must sometimes collide. Good output distribution and no practical structural shortcuts make finding a collision expensive. The generic birthday bound is roughly 2^(n/2) work to find any pair; finding an input for a particular digest is a different preimage problem. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) produces 256 bits (64 hexadecimal characters), with an ideal generic collision bound around 2^128. MD5 and SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm)-1 demonstrate that not every hash is collision resistant. Collision resistant never means collision impossible.

checks.correct: Hash links plus validation and consensus create a shared tamper-evident history
distractors: Encryption alone makes every transaction private
A nonce is the owner’s password
Every blockchain must use Bitcoin mining
checks.teach: Hashes connect history; signatures authorize spending; consensus resolves competing histories. None does all three jobs alone.
checks.answer: Transactions are grouped into blocks. A block header commits to transaction data through a Merkle root and includes the previous block’s hash. Altering data changes its hash and breaks later commitments. Nodes validate transactions and consensus determines the accepted history. In Bitcoin, proof of work requires miners to search nonces for a header hash meeting a target; the accepted valid chain has the greatest cumulative work. More confirmations make rewriting history harder under the network’s security assumptions. Benefits include shared auditability and tamper evidence. Costs include proof-of-work energy use, throughput/latency limits, public-data privacy issues, key loss, and difficult correction of erroneous entries. Blockchain is not an absolute guarantee of truth or immutability, and not all blockchains use proof of work.

checks.q: A retailer inspects gateway traffic, segments payment systems, collects endpoint events, and uses redundant devices to avoid a single outage. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Inspect traffic at controlled entry points, collect useful records, provide backup paths, and plan for growing traffic.
distractors: A perimeter firewall eliminates all endpoint risk
Visibility means capturing only public web pages
Redundancy makes filtering rules unnecessary
checks.teach: A choke point is a controlled place where traffic passes. Visibility means collecting evidence of activity. Availability means keeping services working. Scalability means handling growth. For example, a store checks traffic entering its network, keeps payment computers separate from other systems, records activity on staff devices, and provides a backup network device so one failure does not stop sales.
checks.answer: Use safeguards at both perimeter and endpoint. A choke point is a controlled entry or exit where traffic can be inspected; internal segmentation also matters. Visibility requires useful telemetry at these boundaries and on hosts. Redundancy reduces single points of failure, while scalability supports changing workload. Balance security with business availability, budget, and capacity.

checks.q: An alert-only sensor reports suspicious traffic. An inline prevention rule blocks the same traffic, potentially interrupting legitimate service if the rule is wrong. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: An IDS detects suspicious activity and alerts; an IPS can also block or interrupt suspicious activity.
distractors: IDS always blocks packets
IPS always requires AI
An antivirus database makes false negatives impossible
checks.teach: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) stands for Intrusion Detection System. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) stands for Intrusion Prevention System. Detection raises an alert. Prevention can take action to stop activity. Both need careful rules so normal work is not mistaken for an attack.
checks.answer: An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) detects suspicious activity and alerts. An IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) can actively block or disrupt traffic or activity. Either can use signatures, heuristics, behavior, or other techniques; an IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) does not require AI. Host IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) observes local activity; network controls observe traffic. Tune false positives and false negatives in light of business impact.

checks.q: An analyst finds a long outbound connection in flow logs, examines available packet evidence, then correlates it with proxy and endpoint events. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Packet capture stores packet bytes; flow records summarize connections; a proxy handles requests; allowlisting controls which programs run.
distractors: Flow records always include every file
A proxy is the same as PCAP
Allowlisting permits all unknown programs
checks.teach: Packet capture records observed packet contents within recording limits. Flow records summarize who communicated, when, and how much. A proxy receives and forwards application requests while applying rules. Application allowlisting prevents unapproved programs from running. These are four different jobs.
checks.answer: Full PCAP (Packet Capture) records packet bytes within capture limits, useful for detailed reconstruction; encrypted payloads remain encrypted without suitable keys. Flow records summarize conversations such as endpoints, times, ports, and byte counts. A proxy mediates application requests and can enforce policy and log activity. Application allowlisting permits approved software and restricts other execution. These controls complement rather than replace one another.

checks.q: A service is unavailable despite modest bandwidth because many connections remain incomplete. Appropriate connection limits and timeouts address this pattern. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: They consume connection resources and deny legitimate access
distractors: All DoS attacks require a giant botnet
Slowloris encrypts a database
A SYN flood is simply a race condition
checks.teach: Bandwidth floods and application connection exhaustion stress different resources. Match mitigation to the bottleneck.
checks.answer: Denial of service exhausts resources or disrupts access; distributed DoS (Denial of Service) uses multiple sources. A SYN flood abuses half-open TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection state. Slowloris holds many HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) connections with incomplete, slow requests and may work from few sources. Mitigations include upstream filtering, rate and connection limits, appropriate timeouts, SYN protections, and capacity planning. DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) can distract responders but is not always a distraction or a race condition.

checks.q: A search value must remain a SQL parameter. A comment displayed on a page must remain text or sanitized allowed HTML rather than executable script. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: SQLi changes query interpretation; XSS executes script in the browser
distractors: Both are prevented by antivirus alone
XSS always takes full control of the application server
Prepared statements alone prevent every XSS flaw
checks.teach: Ask where the injected content is interpreted: database query engine or victim browser. XSS (Cross Site Scripting) is not automatically full server control.
checks.answer: SQL (Structured Query Language) injection makes untrusted input influence database query structure. Parameterized queries keep data separate from SQL (Structured Query Language) commands; least-privilege database accounts limit harm. XSS (Cross Site Scripting) causes attacker-controlled script to execute in a user’s browser in a trusted site’s context. Use context-aware output encoding, safe APIs, and appropriate sanitization for allowed HTML (Hypertext Markup Language). Input validation supports both but is insufficient alone. WebGoat is a deliberately vulnerable teaching application. Neither attack is limited to one operating system.

checks.correct: Structured testing and social-engineering simulation reveal technical and human weaknesses
distractors: SET is a hash algorithm
Patching alone prevents every fake-login attack
A captured password always means code executed on the host

checks.answer: Metasploit organizes authorized security testing through exploit, payload, auxiliary, and post-exploitation capabilities. The credential-harvesting lab demonstrates how user trust can disclose credentials without a software exploit. Prevent with training, filtering, phishing-resistant MFA (Multi Factor Authentication), and login monitoring. If credentials are disclosed, report, reset affected secrets from a trusted device, revoke sessions, and investigate related access.

checks.q: The lab’s isolated victim records test keystrokes. An organization should investigate the endpoint and account access rather than assume HTTPS prevented disclosure. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: The endpoint can capture keystrokes before transport encryption
distractors: HTTPS disables all keyboard monitoring
All keyloggers are network routers
Only encrypted keystrokes can be logged
checks.teach: Protection during transmission does not protect the moment data is typed on a compromised device.
checks.answer: A keylogger records input on the endpoint, often before TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts it for transport. Software variants may intercept input APIs, run with elevated privileges, or observe forms; hardware variants can sit between keyboard and computer. Defend with endpoint monitoring, least privilege, updates, application controls, physical inspection where appropriate, and phishing-resistant authentication. Transport encryption alone cannot secure a compromised endpoint.

Public-key encryption uses the recipient’s public key and recipient’s private key to decrypt. Signing uses the sender’s private key and verification uses the sender’s public key. AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is symmetric; RSA (Rivest Shamir Adleman) and ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) belong to asymmetric families. checks.q: A voice application may prioritize timely delivery over retransmitting old audio; a file transfer needs all bytes. Both rely on IP routing. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: TCP delivers an ordered byte stream with recovery; UDP sends separate messages without those guarantees; IP forwards packets toward destinations.
distractors: IP guarantees every byte in order
UDP is only allowed on private networks
TCP stands for Transportation Control Protocol
checks.teach: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) puts received bytes in order and retransmits missing data when possible. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) sends individual messages called datagrams without automatically recovering missing messages or putting them in order. IP (Internet Protocol) handles addressing and forwarding packets between networks; best effort means it does not promise delivery.
checks.answer: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) provides a reliable ordered byte stream, using SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK for conventional connection establishment. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) provides datagrams without TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)-style delivery or ordering guarantees and is useful where applications tolerate loss or implement their own recovery. Both operate at the transport layer. IP (Internet Protocol) addresses and routes packets at the network layer with best-effort delivery. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is not restricted to private networks, and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) does not guarantee timeliness or encryption. Packet lengths can vary.

checks.q: A name resolves unexpectedly, so an analyst checks DNS evidence and validation. Separate authentication logs and packet metadata help establish the incident timeline. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: DNS looks up names; SNMP manages devices; ICMP carries network diagnostic/control messages; FTP transfers files; SMTP sends mail; POP retrieves mail.
distractors: DNSSEC encrypts every website
FTP always uses port 20 for all traffic
ICMP is a mail retrieval service
checks.teach: Each protocol defines rules for a different communication task. DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) adds authentication of signed DNS (Domain Name System) data, not encryption of ordinary queries. Traditional FTP (File Transfer Protocol) does not encrypt its transfers. A protocol’s name alone does not mean its traffic is confidential.
checks.answer: DNS (Domain Name System) resolves names and other records; poisoning supplies false resolution information. DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) authenticates signed DNS (Domain Name System) data and integrity when correctly validated, without encrypting ordinary DNS (Domain Name System) queries. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) monitors and manages devices; v3 supports stronger protection. ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) carries network control and diagnostic messages, including ping. checks.q: A lost powered-off encrypted laptop needs storage protection. A compromised running session exposes data in use, so disk encryption alone is insufficient. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Full-disk encryption protects stored data when the keys remain protected.
distractors: Steganography always encrypts content
A TPM prevents every software exploit
Forward secrecy means keys never change
checks.teach: Full-disk encryption protects data saved on the drive. It does not prevent every attack after the device is unlocked. Other Chapter 3 concepts have separate definition questions, including steganography, forward secrecy, TPM (Trusted Platform Module), HSM (Hardware Security Module), and stream and block ciphers.
checks.answer: Steganography hides the existence of data; encryption hides readable content. ROT13 is a substitution cipher, and XOR gives 0 for equal input bits and 1 for different bits. Stream ciphers process streams; block ciphers process fixed-size blocks. Diffusion spreads a plaintext change through the output; confusion obscures the relation between key and ciphertext. Secure randomness and key management matter. Diffie-Hellman establishes a shared secret; ephemeral exchanges can support forward secrecy when used correctly. Downgrade attacks force weaker options. TPM (Trusted Platform Module) and HSM (Hardware Security Module) protect cryptographic operations and keys; full-disk encryption protects stored data. Resource, power, and latency constraints influence implementation choices.

checks.q: Which control best fits an IP block, a website category policy, or unapproved execution?
checks.correct: Firewall or ACL rules for an IP address; a filtering proxy for websites; application allowlisting for program execution.
distractors: A passive IDS alone guarantees all blocks
PCAP alone prevents execution

checks.q: How do signature detection, anomaly detection, and tuning affect decisions?

distractors: Every anomaly is malicious
Every signature is guaranteed unique
A zero alert rate proves perfect security

checks.answer: Signatures recognize described patterns. Anomaly detection compares activity with an expected pattern. Both can be wrong.

checks.q: Why do valid signatures alone not solve the double-spending problem?
checks.correct: A signature authorizes a spend; validation and consensus must also prevent the same output from being spent twice.
distractors: A valid signature makes every conflicting spend acceptable
Any chain with more block count is always valid
Every hard fork guarantees two permanent chains
checks.teach: Double spending means trying to use the same digital funds twice. A person controlling a key can sign two conflicting transactions. A valid signature shows authorization, not that the funds remain unspent. Nodes check unspent outputs and agree on a valid history.
checks.answer: The same owner might authorize two conflicting spends. The network needs rules and agreement about which valid history to accept.
checks.example: Two transactions spend the same previous output and both have genuine owner signatures. They cannot both enter the same valid transaction history.

checks.q: How do application data, TCP segments, and IP packets fit together?
checks.correct: Application data is carried in a TCP segment, which is carried in an IP packet, which is carried in a link-layer frame.
distractors: TCP contains the entire Internet routing table
Every IP packet has the same fixed size
IP automatically encrypts the payload
checks.teach: Each layer adds its own control information. The IP (Internet Protocol) payload can include a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) header and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) data. The frame carries the IP (Internet Protocol) packet across a particular local link.
checks.answer: Picture nested envelopes. Each layer adds information for its own job; the whole packet is not just the user’s message.
checks.example: A short message gains TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and IP (Internet Protocol) headers before link transmission. A capture can show ports and addresses even when higher-level contents are encrypted.

setting.location: The application, transport service, IP (Internet Protocol) network, and local links.
setting.purpose: Understand which layer handles reliable delivery, separate messages, and forwarding. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) delivers an ordered byte stream with recovery; UDP (User Datagram Protocol) provides separate datagrams without those guarantees; IP (Internet Protocol) forwards packets toward destinations.
setting.action: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) delivers an ordered byte stream with recovery; UDP (User Datagram Protocol) provides separate datagrams without those guarantees; IP (Internet Protocol) forwards packets toward destinations.

checks.q: How do FTP, FTPS, SFTP, HTTPS, S/MIME, SRTP, and NTP differ?
checks.correct: FTPS protects FTP with TLS; SFTP transfers files over SSH; HTTPS protects web traffic; S/MIME protects email content; SRTP protects media; NTP synchronizes clocks.
distractors: SFTP and FTPS are identical
Plain NTP guarantees authenticated time
DNSSEC encrypts every web connection
checks.teach: Start with the application task, then identify its protection. FTPS (File Transfer Protocol over Transport Layer Security) and SFTP (Secure Shell File Transfer Protocol) use different protocols. Ordinary NTP (Network Time Protocol) does not automatically provide cryptographic protection. A secure-looking name is not a substitute for checking how the service is actually configured.
checks.answer: Similar names can hide different protocols. Choose the protection and application first.
checks.example: A company moving files chooses SFTP (Secure Shell File Transfer Protocol) over SSH (Secure Shell). A signed email may remain signed beyond one transport connection, unlike merely protecting its delivery link with TLS (Transport Layer Security).

checks.q: How do access audit event and security logs support an investigation?

distractors: One log contains every action forever
No retained event proves nothing happened
All file changes are definitely malicious

checks.answer: Each log is a partial witness. Put the witnesses on a common timeline and preserve the evidence needed to explain what happened.

A file containing exactly “Amount: 90” has digest e24d0dad16f71dd46ada00ca89aa14fc46afe38f8907c1d93b7af14c6ff785ac. If the first digest is the publisher’s trusted reference but the download produces the second, the contents differ. The program compares these values; neither value is decrypted to recover the text. cloze.q: SHA-256 produces a digest containing _____ bits.
cloze.answer: Qualify the premise: a well-designed cryptographic hash aims for computational collision resistance. A fixed n-bit digest has 2^n possible outputs, so different inputs must sometimes collide. Good output distribution and no practical structural shortcuts make finding a collision expensive. The generic birthday bound is roughly 2^(n/2) work to find any pair; finding an input for a particular digest is a different preimage problem. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) produces 256 bits (64 hexadecimal characters), with an ideal generic collision bound around 2^128. MD5 and SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm)-1 demonstrate that not every hash is collision resistant. Collision resistant never means collision impossible.
cloze.teach: A large output space makes a matching pair hard to find, but fixed-length outputs cannot uniquely represent every possible input.
cloze.example: Two distinct files could share a digest. A trusted expected hash can help verify a download, but an attacker changing both file and untrusted posted hash defeats that simple comparison.

cloze.q: Miners vary a _____ while searching for valid proof of work.
distractors: Password
Public key
Checksum
cloze.answer: A proof-of-work nonce is a value miners vary while searching for a block-header hash meeting a target. A Merkle root commits to the block’s transactions using a tree of hashes. cloze.q: The handshake order is SYN, _____, ACK.
distractors: FIN
DNS
UDP
cloze.answer: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) provides a reliable ordered byte stream, using SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK for conventional connection establishment. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) provides datagrams without TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)-style delivery or ordering guarantees and is useful where applications tolerate loss or implement their own recovery. Both operate at the transport layer. IP (Internet Protocol) addresses and routes packets at the network layer with best-effort delivery. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is not restricted to private networks, and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) does not guarantee timeliness or encryption. Packet lengths can vary.
cloze.teach: Reliability, latency tradeoffs, and routing are separate design concerns.
cloze.example: A voice application may prioritize timely delivery over retransmitting old audio; a file transfer needs all bytes. Both rely on IP (Internet Protocol) routing.

cloze.answer: A keylogger records input on the endpoint, often before TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts it for transport. Software variants may intercept input APIs, run with elevated privileges, or observe forms; hardware variants can sit between keyboard and computer. Not every keylogger requires process injection or admin rights. Defend with endpoint monitoring, least privilege, updates, application controls, physical inspection where appropriate, and phishing-resistant authentication. Transport encryption alone cannot secure a compromised endpoint.
cloze.teach: Protection during transmission does not protect the moment data is typed on a compromised device.

walkthrough.starting: A downloaded file and a digest supplied through a trusted source for the original file.
walkthrough.operation: A hash program reads the downloaded file’s bytes and performs the hash calculation on them.
walkthrough.result: A fixed-length sequence of bits called a digest, commonly displayed as letters and digits. The digest is a separate computed value, not a replacement for the file.
walkthrough.use: A person or program compares the computed digest with the trusted reference. Different digests mean different contents. A match supports a content match under the hash’s security assumptions; it does not alone prove that the file is safe or who published it.
walkthrough.workedExample: A file containing exactly the text “Amount: 10” has SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) digest 8c8b27520e4a1ce517751f52fff50a3473edc4a9f1cedefcd4e2c379ac9ce0f8. A file containing exactly “Amount: 90” has digest e24d0dad16f71dd46ada00ca89aa14fc46afe38f8907c1d93b7af14c6ff785ac. If the first digest is the publisher’s trusted reference but the download produces the second, the contents differ. The program compares these values; neither value is decrypted to recover the text. These example files have no trailing newline.

vocab.answer: The fixed-length result produced by a hash function: a compact summary used for comparison. It is not the original file or an encrypted copy of it.
vocab.teach: The program reads the supplied data and calculates a fixed-length value. The useful next step is comparison with a trusted reference value to check contents. The value is not a readable explanation of the file, an encrypted copy, or proof of the publisher’s identity.
vocab.example: A publisher provides a trusted reference hash for a particular installer, and a user checks a downloaded copy. The checker computes the downloaded contents’ hash using the named method and compares values. A match supports matching contents under the hash assumptions; a mismatch shows different contents. Neither result alone certifies harmless software.
vocab.correct: The fixed-length result produced by a hash function: a compact summary used for comparison. It is not the original file or an encrypted copy of it.
distractors: A reversibly encrypted message
An owner’s secret signing exponent
A network device access list

setting.object: A publisher provides a trusted reference hash for a particular installer, and a user checks a downloaded copy.
setting.location: The original release, the downloaded file’s bytes, and the trusted reference value.
setting.purpose: Compute or evaluate a summary of contents so it can be compared with a trusted reference. For a downloaded file, the purpose is to check whether its contents match the original; this does not hide the file or by itself prove who published it.
setting.action: The checker computes the downloaded contents’ hash using the named method and compares values.
setting.example: A match supports matching contents under the hash assumptions; a mismatch shows different contents. Neither result alone certifies harmless software.

walkthrough.starting: A publisher provides a trusted reference hash for a particular installer, and a user checks a downloaded copy.
walkthrough.operation: The checker computes the downloaded contents’ hash using the named method and compares values.
walkthrough.result: A match supports matching contents under the hash assumptions; a mismatch shows different contents. Neither result alone certifies harmless software.
walkthrough.use: Compute or evaluate a summary of contents so it can be compared with a trusted reference. For a downloaded file, the purpose is to check whether its contents match the original; this does not hide the file or by itself prove who published it.
walkthrough.workedExample: A file containing exactly the text “Amount: 10” has SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) digest 8c8b27520e4a1ce517751f52fff50a3473edc4a9f1cedefcd4e2c379ac9ce0f8. A file containing exactly “Amount: 90” has digest e24d0dad16f71dd46ada00ca89aa14fc46afe38f8907c1d93b7af14c6ff785ac. If the first digest is the publisher’s trusted reference but the download produces the second, the contents differ. The program compares these values; neither value is decrypted to recover the text. These example files have no trailing newline.

walkthrough.workedExample: A file containing exactly the text “Amount: 10” has SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) digest 8c8b27520e4a1ce517751f52fff50a3473edc4a9f1cedefcd4e2c379ac9ce0f8. A file containing exactly “Amount: 90” has digest e24d0dad16f71dd46ada00ca89aa14fc46afe38f8907c1d93b7af14c6ff785ac. If the first digest is the publisher’s trusted reference but the download produces the second, the contents differ. The program compares these values; neither value is decrypted to recover the text. These example files have no trailing newline.

timeline.event: Keeps a trusted earlier baseline, recalculates the file’s hash later, and compares the new value with that earlier reference. This is a second scenario; not every system performs it automatically.

vocab.correct: A procedure that turns input information into a fixed-length result called a digest. It is not encryption and has no decryption operation.
vocab.answer: A procedure that turns input information into a fixed-length result called a digest. It is not encryption and has no decryption operation.
vocab.teach: The program reads the supplied data and calculates a fixed-length value. The useful next step is comparison with a trusted reference value to check contents. The value is not a readable explanation of the file, an encrypted copy, or proof of the publisher’s identity.
vocab.example: A publisher provides a trusted reference hash for a particular installer, and a user checks a downloaded copy. The checker computes the downloaded contents’ hash using the named method and compares values. A match supports matching contents under the hash assumptions; a mismatch shows different contents. Neither result alone certifies harmless software.

walkthrough.operation: The checker computes the downloaded contents’ hash using the named method and compares values.

walkthrough.use: Compute or evaluate a summary of contents so it can be compared with a trusted reference. For a downloaded file, the purpose is to check whether its contents match the original; this does not hide the file or by itself prove who published it.
walkthrough.workedExample: A file containing exactly the text “Amount: 10” has SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) digest 8c8b27520e4a1ce517751f52fff50a3473edc4a9f1cedefcd4e2c379ac9ce0f8. A file containing exactly “Amount: 90” has digest e24d0dad16f71dd46ada00ca89aa14fc46afe38f8907c1d93b7af14c6ff785ac. If the first digest is the publisher’s trusted reference but the download produces the second, the contents differ. The program compares these values; neither value is decrypted to recover the text. These example files have no trailing newline.

timeline.when: Before the download is offered
timeline.event: Finalizes the original release file. The file’s exact bytes are the contents that recipients should obtain.

timeline.when: Before or when the release is published
timeline.event: Reads the original file and computes a reference hash using a named method such as SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest). The publisher makes that reference available through a trusted release channel.

timeline.when: You download the release
timeline.event: Transfers the file to your computer. A download by itself does not imply that a separate reference-hash comparison has happened.

timeline.when: You or a configured verification tool initiates checking
timeline.event: Reads the downloaded file’s bytes and computes its hash using the same method as the publisher. It is not comparing the file with itself.

timeline.when: Both values are available
timeline.event: Compares your computed value with the trusted reference value for that exact release. A different version of the legitimate file needs its own reference.

timeline.when: The values differ
timeline.who: Person or system deciding whether to use the file
timeline.event: Treats the contents as different from the trusted original and investigates or obtains the correct file. The mismatch does not explain whether the cause was corruption, a legitimate edit, or malicious alteration.

timeline.when: The values match
timeline.event: Has evidence supporting a content match under the hash’s security assumptions. The match alone is not a guarantee that the file is harmless, or proof of its publisher if the reference was untrusted.

timeline.when: Checking for later changes instead of checking a download
timeline.who: A file-integrity monitoring system or administrator
timeline.event: Keeps a trusted earlier baseline, recalculates the file’s hash later, and compares the new value with that earlier reference. This is a second scenario; not every system performs it automatically.

walkthrough.starting: Application data that one computer needs to send to another.

walkthrough.starting: A readable report saved on a laptop, an encryption procedure, and the required key.
walkthrough.operation: Encryption software reads the report’s data and transforms it using the key.
walkthrough.result: Encrypted bytes called ciphertext. A protected copy may be saved or sent; the application’s design determines what happens to the original.
walkthrough.use: An authorized application later uses the appropriate decryption procedure and key to recover the readable report. Protecting the key helps keep other people from reading the encrypted contents.

timeline.when: Before protecting the report
timeline.event: Identifies the file and who should be allowed to read it, then selects an appropriate encryption feature.

timeline.when: Encryption is requested or automatically required by that feature
timeline.event: Obtains the required key material and transforms the readable file data into ciphertext. Where the key is generated, stored, or unlocked depends on the system.

timeline.when: Saving or sending the protected data
timeline.event: Stores or transmits the encrypted representation and handles keys according to its design. A separate unprotected original must also be considered.

timeline.when: An authorized person later opens the information
timeline.event: Uses the appropriate decryption procedure and key to recover readable contents. A running application may now have plaintext in memory, which needs its own access protection.

walkthrough.starting: A downloaded file and a digest supplied through a trusted source for the original file.
walkthrough.operation: A hash program reads the downloaded file’s bytes and performs the hash calculation on them.
walkthrough.result: A fixed-length sequence of bits called a digest, commonly displayed as letters and digits. The digest is a separate computed value, not a replacement for the file.
walkthrough.use: A person or program compares the computed digest with the trusted reference. Different digests mean different contents. A match supports a content match under the hash’s security assumptions; it does not alone prove that the file is safe or who published it.
walkthrough.workedExample: A file containing exactly the text “Amount: 10” has SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) digest 8c8b27520e4a1ce517751f52fff50a3473edc4a9f1cedefcd4e2c379ac9ce0f8. A file containing exactly “Amount: 90” has digest e24d0dad16f71dd46ada00ca89aa14fc46afe38f8907c1d93b7af14c6ff785ac. If the first digest is the publisher’s trusted reference but the download produces the second, the contents differ. The program compares these values; neither value is decrypted to recover the text. These example files have no trailing newline.

timeline.when: Before the download is offered
timeline.event: Finalizes the original release file. The file’s exact bytes are the contents that recipients should obtain.

timeline.when: Before or when the release is published
timeline.event: Reads the original file and computes a reference hash using a named method such as SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest). The publisher makes that reference available through a trusted release channel.

timeline.when: You download the release
timeline.event: Transfers the file to your computer. A download by itself does not imply that a separate reference-hash comparison has happened.

timeline.when: You or a configured verification tool initiates checking
timeline.event: Reads the downloaded file’s bytes and computes its hash using the same method as the publisher. It is not comparing the file with itself.

timeline.when: Both values are available
timeline.event: Compares your computed value with the trusted reference value for that exact release. A different version of the legitimate file needs its own reference.

timeline.when: The values differ
timeline.who: Person or system deciding whether to use the file
timeline.event: Treats the contents as different from the trusted original and investigates or obtains the correct file. The mismatch does not explain whether the cause was corruption, a legitimate edit, or malicious alteration.

timeline.when: The values match
timeline.event: Has evidence supporting a content match under the hash’s security assumptions. The match alone is not a guarantee that the file is harmless, or proof of its publisher if the reference was untrusted.

timeline.when: Checking for later changes instead of checking a download
timeline.who: A file-integrity monitoring system or administrator
timeline.event: Keeps a trusted earlier baseline, recalculates the file’s hash later, and compares the new value with that earlier reference. This is a second scenario; not every system performs it automatically.

The guide points at Chapter 1. Detailed virus types in this edition are Chapter 2, pp. 55–65.
Script runs in a victim browser in the site context. It does not inherently grant full application-server control.
Fixed-length digests are not guaranteed unique. Plain hashes do not establish sender identity.
Recipient keys protect confidentiality; sender keys sign and verify. Signing is not generally described as encrypting with a private key.
Choose e coprime to φ(n), not merely coprime to n. Use ed ≡ 1 mod φ(n).
Transmission Control Protocol provides reliability, not encryption. Its Internet checksum is not a cryptographic SHA digest.
MFA reduces password-only compromise but does not stop every phishing or session attack. HTTPS cannot protect data already exposed on a compromised endpoint.
Pseudonymity is not anonymity. Prefer greatest cumulative proof of work to a simplistic longest-by-block-count rule.
IPS does not require AI. Allowlisting is a control concept, not inherently obsolete.
Professor guide estimates 15 T/F, 20 MC, 10 blanks, 5–7 discussions. October 15 notes give ranges of 10–15, 20–25, 10–12, 5–7. Neither is an exact promise.
All eight lecture decks are now directly reviewed. Lectures 2–4 were recovered from PPTs_export.zip; the duplicate Lecture 3 copy has identical extracted slide/note text.
AES uses 128-bit blocks and 128/192/256-bit keys with total rounds 10/12/14. Keep block size separate from key size and the textbook’s middle-round count.
TPM and HSM are different categories. Hardware is not immune to every implementation or firmware attack.
SFTP is over SSH; FTPS adds TLS to FTP. Plain NTP is not automatically authenticated. S/MIME capability depends on the client and key setup.
Old screenshots, prices, percentages, vendor support schedules, and legal penalties are not presented as current facts or required memorization.
The lecture’s 65-bit hexadecimal phrase is incorrect. A SHA-256 digest has 256 bits, typically displayed as 64 hexadecimal characters.

If the first digest is the publisher’s trusted reference but the download produces the second, the contents differ. The program compares these values; neither value is decrypted to recover the text. primer.meaning: A computer or device on which programs run, such as a laptop or server.
A server provides a service; a client requests it. One device can perform both roles.
The OS (Operating System) manages the device’s resources. An application performs a task using those resources.
A network connects devices. A protocol gives rules for their communication.
A packet carries data. Its header carries control information; its payload is the carried content, which can itself contain another layer’s header.
An IP (Internet Protocol) address identifies a network endpoint; a port helps identify a transport service or conversation.
A vulnerability is a weakness. An exploit takes advantage of it. A payload is the action or code delivered or run.
Authentication checks a claimed identity. Authorization decides what that identity may do.
A firewall enforces communication rules. Detection identifies suspicious activity; an alert needs investigation.
A key controls a cryptographic operation. A hash is a digest for comparison. A signature provides verifiable authorization or origin under a trusted key.
A public key may be distributed. Its corresponding private key must stay secret. Which person’s key you use depends on the goal.
Explain what information, money, service, or trust is at risk, and why your proposed defense addresses it.
A transaction records a transfer or other event. A ledger is the record of those events.
A block groups records and control information. A blockchain links blocks using cryptographic commitments to earlier history.
Validation checks the rules. Consensus is how participants agree on an accepted history despite competing or faulty participants.
Distributed work or storage is spread across systems. Decentralized authority is spread across decision makers. A distributed system can still be centrally controlled.

discussions.title: Why patching becomes easier
discussions.q: How do bandwidth, cloud computing, big data/analytics, and virtualization alleviate security-update pressure?
discussions.answer: More bandwidth speeds patch distribution, although deployments still need scheduling. Cloud-based and centralized management can coordinate updates across fleets, while customers retain responsibilities for their own systems and configurations. Analytics helps inventory systems, prioritize exposure, and detect failed updates. Virtualization supports representative test environments, snapshots, and rollback. Together these reduce transfer, coordination, decision, and testing costs. They do not remove compatibility testing, outages, or zero-day risk.
discussions.teach: Organize your discussion by the bottleneck each technology reduces. State one benefit and one limitation for each.
discussions.example: A business inventories vulnerable devices, prioritizes exposed servers, tests a patch on representative VMs, pilots deployment, monitors failures, and rolls out in stages with rollback available.
discussions.correct: Distribution, coordination, prioritization, and safe testing become easier
distractors: All updates can be installed without testing
Snapshots eliminate the need for backups
Cloud providers automatically patch every customer application

discussions.title: Viruses and other malware
discussions.q: What are the major types of computer viruses, and how do virus, worm, scareware, adware, spyware, and backdoor differ?
discussions.answer: A virus attaches to a host file or document and replicates when the host runs; a worm is a standalone program that can propagate across networks. Scareware uses fraudulent alarms to pressure payment or installation. Adware displays unwanted advertising; spyware secretly collects information; a backdoor bypasses normal access controls. In this textbook’s Chapter 2, viruses include program/file viruses and macro viruses, with appender infection and armored concealment techniques: Swiss cheese, split infection, oligomorphic, polymorphic, and metamorphic mutation. Boot-sector viruses are another common category, but the supplied edition emphasizes the preceding list. The guide labels this Ch. 1; the relevant detail is actually Ch. 2, pp. 55–65.
discussions.teach: Compare how malware spreads, hides, and acts. These categories can overlap: a backdoor may install spyware that includes a keylogger.
discussions.example: An infected document executes a malicious macro; a network worm spreads independently; a fake antivirus page scares a user into paying. Each has a different mechanism and defense.
discussions.correct: Virus needs a host; worm propagates independently; other names describe behavior
distractors: All malware is a virus
Scareware is legitimate antivirus
Backdoors are the same as checksums

discussions.title: Confidentiality authentication obfuscation
discussions.q: How do confidentiality, authentication, and obfuscation correlate in cryptographic applications?
discussions.answer: Confidentiality limits who can read data, usually through encryption. Authentication establishes a claimed identity or data origin through a suitable cryptographic protocol; a digital signature can bind a message to a signing key. Obfuscation makes information or implementation details harder to understand, and the textbook includes it among cryptographic protections. These goals complement one another but do not substitute for one another. Encryption to a recipient’s public key does not by itself identify the sender; an ordinary hash does not authenticate an origin; signing does not encrypt the message. For secrecy plus sender authentication, use a properly designed encrypted and authenticated scheme.
discussions.teach: Ask three separate questions: who can read, who created or approved it, and what details are being obscured?
discussions.example: A sender signs a document with the sender’s private signing key and protects the content for the recipient. The recipient decrypts and verifies using the appropriate keys and a trusted identity binding.
discussions.correct: Encryption protects reading; authentication proves origin; obfuscation obscures details
distractors: A hash alone proves the sender
A signature automatically hides the message
Obfuscation always replaces encryption
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage

discussions.title: Collision resistance
discussions.q: Hash algorithms are naturally resistant to hash collisions. Why?
discussions.answer: Qualify the premise: a well-designed cryptographic hash aims for computational collision resistance. A fixed n-bit digest has 2^n possible outputs, so different inputs must sometimes collide. Good output distribution and no practical structural shortcuts make finding a collision expensive. The generic birthday bound is roughly 2^(n/2) work to find any pair; finding an input for a particular digest is a different preimage problem. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) produces 256 bits (64 hexadecimal characters), with an ideal generic collision bound around 2^128. MD5 and SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm)-1 demonstrate that not every hash is collision resistant. Collision resistant never means collision impossible.
discussions.teach: A large output space makes a matching pair hard to find, but fixed-length outputs cannot uniquely represent every possible input.
discussions.example: Two distinct files could share a digest. A trusted expected hash can help verify a download, but an attacker changing both file and untrusted posted hash defeats that simple comparison.
discussions.correct: Large well-distributed outputs make finding collisions computationally difficult
distractors: Collisions are mathematically impossible
Hashing encrypts every input uniquely
All hash algorithms have equal collision resistance

discussions.title: Blockchain mechanics and tradeoffs
discussions.q: How does blockchain work? What are its pros and cons?
discussions.answer: Transactions are grouped into blocks. A block header commits to transaction data through a Merkle root and includes the previous block’s hash. Altering data changes its hash and breaks later commitments. Nodes validate transactions and consensus determines the accepted history. In Bitcoin, proof of work requires miners to search nonces for a header hash meeting a target; the accepted valid chain has the greatest cumulative work. More confirmations make rewriting history harder under the network’s security assumptions. Benefits include shared auditability and tamper evidence. Costs include proof-of-work energy use, throughput/latency limits, public-data privacy issues, key loss, and difficult correction of erroneous entries. Blockchain is not an absolute guarantee of truth or immutability, and not all blockchains use proof of work.
discussions.teach: Hashes connect history; signatures authorize spending; consensus resolves competing histories. None does all three jobs alone.
discussions.example: Change an old record in a teaching chain. Its hash and descendants no longer match. Rehashing a local copy is easy in a toy demo; convincing a real consensus network is the costly part.
discussions.correct: Hash links plus validation and consensus create a shared tamper-evident history
distractors: Encryption alone makes every transaction private
A nonce is the owner’s password
Every blockchain must use Bitcoin mining

discussions.title: Bitcoin and ownership transfer
discussions.answer: Bitcoin is a peer-to-peer digital currency whose transaction history is recorded on a blockchain. A spender authorizes use of earlier unspent transaction outputs by satisfying their spending conditions, typically with a digital signature created using the spender’s private key. A new output specifies conditions for the receiver. Nodes verify authorization and check for double spending; mining orders valid transactions through proof of work. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) contributes to hashing and proof of work, not encryption of a coin. An address is commonly derived from a key or script and is not always the raw public key. Public ledger transparency provides pseudonymity, not guaranteed anonymity. Miners receive a block subsidy and transaction fees as incentives.
discussions.teach: Ownership means the ability to authorize spending under the output’s rules. You transfer spending rights through a transaction; you do not email a secret coin file.
discussions.example: Alice signs a transaction spending an output she controls and creating one for Bob. Others verify it with public information. Bob later spends by satisfying his output’s conditions.
discussions.correct: A peer-to-peer currency with signature-authorized spending and blockchain consensus
distractors: A coin encrypted with SHA-256 and emailed
A central-bank database with no signatures
An anonymous password shared by all miners

discussions.title: Metasploit and SET business case
discussions.q: A staff member used a fake login page, then the workstation made an unusual outbound connection. Explain the possible business impact, useful evidence, and layered response.
discussions.answer: The fake login may have disclosed credentials, putting accounts and accessible business records at risk. The unusual connection warrants investigation but does not alone prove a reverse shell or data theft. Correlate the login timeline, endpoint processes and files, destination details, and available proxy, flow, and packet evidence. Follow the incident plan to contain affected systems and preserve evidence; reset compromised credentials from a trusted device, revoke sessions, and investigate related account activity. Endpoint execution may require host recovery in addition to account remediation. Prevent recurrence with independent verification, filtering, phishing-resistant authentication, least privilege, patching, application controls, EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), and appropriate egress policy. Explain the distinct limits: patches do not stop every fake login, TLS (Transport Layer Security) does not fix an already compromised endpoint, and an outbound connection is not automatically trusted.
discussions.teach: Explain the weakness, business consequence, evidence, and defense. Exact tool-menu commands are not the stated exam priority.
discussions.example: A fake staff login collects a test password in the isolated lab. A business analogue is account takeover leading to exposed records or fraudulent actions.
discussions.correct: Structured testing and social-engineering simulation reveal technical and human weaknesses
distractors: SET is a hash algorithm
Patching alone prevents every fake-login attack
A captured password always means code executed on the host

walkthrough.starting: A downloaded file and a digest supplied through a trusted source for the original file.
walkthrough.operation: A hash program reads the downloaded file’s bytes and performs the hash calculation on them.
walkthrough.result: A fixed-length sequence of bits called a digest, commonly displayed as letters and digits. The digest is a separate computed value, not a replacement for the file.
walkthrough.use: A person or program compares the computed digest with the trusted reference. Different digests mean different contents. A match supports a content match under the hash’s security assumptions; it does not alone prove that the file is safe or who published it.
walkthrough.workedExample: A file containing exactly the text “Amount: 10” has SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) digest 8c8b27520e4a1ce517751f52fff50a3473edc4a9f1cedefcd4e2c379ac9ce0f8. A file containing exactly “Amount: 90” has digest e24d0dad16f71dd46ada00ca89aa14fc46afe38f8907c1d93b7af14c6ff785ac. If the first digest is the publisher’s trusted reference but the download produces the second, the contents differ. The program compares these values; neither value is decrypted to recover the text. These example files have no trailing newline.

foundations.answer: The fixed-length result produced by a hash function: a compact summary used for comparison. It is not the original file or an encrypted copy of it.
foundations.teach: The program reads the supplied data and calculates a fixed-length value. The useful next step is comparison with a trusted reference value to check contents. The value is not a readable explanation of the file, an encrypted copy, or proof of the publisher’s identity.
foundations.example: A publisher provides a trusted reference hash for a particular installer, and a user checks a downloaded copy. The checker computes the downloaded contents’ hash using the named method and compares values. A match supports matching contents under the hash assumptions; a mismatch shows different contents. Neither result alone certifies harmless software.
foundations.correct: The fixed-length result produced by a hash function: a compact summary used for comparison. It is not the original file or an encrypted copy of it.
distractors: Rivest Shamir Adleman. An asymmetric cryptographic family named for Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman. Classroom arithmetic uses products of primes and modular exponents.
Secure Hash Algorithm. A family of cryptographic hash algorithms. SHA-256 produces a 256-bit digest and is distinct from encryption.
Hash based Message Authentication Code. A keyed hash construction for message integrity and authentication among parties sharing a secret. It does not encrypt the message.

setting.object: A publisher provides a trusted reference hash for a particular installer, and a user checks a downloaded copy.
setting.location: The original release, the downloaded file’s bytes, and the trusted reference value.
setting.purpose: Compute or evaluate a summary of contents so it can be compared with a trusted reference. For a downloaded file, the purpose is to check whether its contents match the original; this does not hide the file or by itself prove who published it.
setting.action: The checker computes the downloaded contents’ hash using the named method and compares values.
setting.example: A match supports matching contents under the hash assumptions; a mismatch shows different contents. Neither result alone certifies harmless software.

walkthrough.use: Compute or evaluate a summary of contents so it can be compared with a trusted reference. For a downloaded file, the purpose is to check whether its contents match the original; this does not hide the file or by itself prove who published it.
walkthrough.workedExample: A file containing exactly the text “Amount: 10” has SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) digest 8c8b27520e4a1ce517751f52fff50a3473edc4a9f1cedefcd4e2c379ac9ce0f8. A file containing exactly “Amount: 90” has digest e24d0dad16f71dd46ada00ca89aa14fc46afe38f8907c1d93b7af14c6ff785ac. If the first digest is the publisher’s trusted reference but the download produces the second, the contents differ. The program compares these values; neither value is decrypted to recover the text. These example files have no trailing newline.

timeline.when: Before the download is offered
timeline.event: Finalizes the original release file. The file’s exact bytes are the contents that recipients should obtain.

timeline.when: Before or when the release is published
timeline.event: Reads the original file and computes a reference hash using a named method such as SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest). The publisher makes that reference available through a trusted release channel.

timeline.when: You download the release
timeline.event: Transfers the file to your computer. A download by itself does not imply that a separate reference-hash comparison has happened.

timeline.when: You or a configured verification tool initiates checking
timeline.event: Reads the downloaded file’s bytes and computes its hash using the same method as the publisher. It is not comparing the file with itself.

timeline.when: Both values are available
timeline.event: Compares your computed value with the trusted reference value for that exact release. A different version of the legitimate file needs its own reference.

timeline.when: The values differ
timeline.who: Person or system deciding whether to use the file
timeline.event: Treats the contents as different from the trusted original and investigates or obtains the correct file. The mismatch does not explain whether the cause was corruption, a legitimate edit, or malicious alteration.

timeline.when: The values match
timeline.event: Has evidence supporting a content match under the hash’s security assumptions. The match alone is not a guarantee that the file is harmless, or proof of its publisher if the reference was untrusted.

timeline.when: Checking for later changes instead of checking a download
timeline.who: A file-integrity monitoring system or administrator
timeline.event: Keeps a trusted earlier baseline, recalculates the file’s hash later, and compares the new value with that earlier reference. This is a second scenario; not every system performs it automatically.

foundations.purpose: Compute or evaluate a summary of contents so it can be compared with a trusted reference. For a downloaded file, the purpose is to check whether its contents match the original; this does not hide the file or by itself prove who published it.

walkthrough.starting: A downloaded file and a digest supplied through a trusted source for the original file.
walkthrough.operation: A hash program reads the downloaded file’s bytes and performs the hash calculation on them.
walkthrough.result: A fixed-length sequence of bits called a digest, commonly displayed as letters and digits. The digest is a separate computed value, not a replacement for the file.
walkthrough.use: A person or program compares the computed digest with the trusted reference. Different digests mean different contents. A match supports a content match under the hash’s security assumptions; it does not alone prove that the file is safe or who published it.
walkthrough.workedExample: A file containing exactly the text “Amount: 10” has SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) digest 8c8b27520e4a1ce517751f52fff50a3473edc4a9f1cedefcd4e2c379ac9ce0f8. A file containing exactly “Amount: 90” has digest e24d0dad16f71dd46ada00ca89aa14fc46afe38f8907c1d93b7af14c6ff785ac. If the first digest is the publisher’s trusted reference but the download produces the second, the contents differ. The program compares these values; neither value is decrypted to recover the text. These example files have no trailing newline.
