walkthrough.workedExample: A file containing exactly the text “Amount: 10” has SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) digest 8c8b27520e4a1ce517751f52fff50a3473edc4a9f1cedefcd4e2c379ac9ce0f8. A file containing exactly “Amount: 90” has digest e24d0dad16f71dd46ada00ca89aa14fc46afe38f8907c1d93b7af14c6ff785ac. If the first digest is the publisher’s trusted reference but the download produces the second, the contents differ. The program compares these values; neither value is decrypted to recover the text. These example files have no trailing newline.

timeline.when: Before the download is offered
timeline.event: Finalizes the original release file. The file’s exact bytes are the contents that recipients should obtain.

timeline.when: Before or when the release is published
timeline.event: Reads the original file and computes a reference hash using a named method such as SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest). The publisher makes that reference available through a trusted release channel.

timeline.when: You download the release
timeline.event: Transfers the file to your computer. A download by itself does not imply that a separate reference-hash comparison has happened.

timeline.when: You or a configured verification tool initiates checking
timeline.event: Reads the downloaded file’s bytes and computes its hash using the same method as the publisher. It is not comparing the file with itself.

timeline.when: Both values are available
timeline.event: Compares your computed value with the trusted reference value for that exact release. A different version of the legitimate file needs its own reference.

timeline.when: The values differ
timeline.who: Person or system deciding whether to use the file
timeline.event: Treats the contents as different from the trusted original and investigates or obtains the correct file. The mismatch does not explain whether the cause was corruption, a legitimate edit, or malicious alteration.

timeline.when: The values match
timeline.event: Has evidence supporting a content match under the hash’s security assumptions. The match alone is not a guarantee that the file is harmless, or proof of its publisher if the reference was untrusted.

timeline.when: Checking for later changes instead of checking a download
timeline.who: A file-integrity monitoring system or administrator
timeline.event: Keeps a trusted earlier baseline, recalculates the file’s hash later, and compares the new value with that earlier reference. This is a second scenario; not every system performs it automatically.

walkthrough.use: A person or program compares the computed digest with the trusted reference. Different digests mean different contents. A match supports a content match under the hash’s security assumptions; it does not alone prove that the file is safe or who published it.
walkthrough.workedExample: A file containing exactly the text “Amount: 10” has SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) digest 8c8b27520e4a1ce517751f52fff50a3473edc4a9f1cedefcd4e2c379ac9ce0f8. A file containing exactly “Amount: 90” has digest e24d0dad16f71dd46ada00ca89aa14fc46afe38f8907c1d93b7af14c6ff785ac. If the first digest is the publisher’s trusted reference but the download produces the second, the contents differ. The program compares these values; neither value is decrypted to recover the text. These example files have no trailing newline.

timeline.when: Before the download is offered
timeline.event: Finalizes the original release file. The file’s exact bytes are the contents that recipients should obtain.

timeline.when: Before or when the release is published
timeline.event: Reads the original file and computes a reference hash using a named method such as SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest). The publisher makes that reference available through a trusted release channel.

timeline.when: You download the release
timeline.event: Transfers the file to your computer. A download by itself does not imply that a separate reference-hash comparison has happened.

timeline.when: You or a configured verification tool initiates checking
timeline.event: Reads the downloaded file’s bytes and computes its hash using the same method as the publisher. It is not comparing the file with itself.

timeline.when: Both values are available
timeline.event: Compares your computed value with the trusted reference value for that exact release. A different version of the legitimate file needs its own reference.

timeline.when: The values differ
timeline.who: Person or system deciding whether to use the file
timeline.event: Treats the contents as different from the trusted original and investigates or obtains the correct file. The mismatch does not explain whether the cause was corruption, a legitimate edit, or malicious alteration.

timeline.when: The values match
timeline.event: Has evidence supporting a content match under the hash’s security assumptions. The match alone is not a guarantee that the file is harmless, or proof of its publisher if the reference was untrusted.

timeline.when: Checking for later changes instead of checking a download
timeline.who: A file-integrity monitoring system or administrator
timeline.event: Keeps a trusted earlier baseline, recalculates the file’s hash later, and compares the new value with that earlier reference. This is a second scenario; not every system performs it automatically.

orientation.q: What is a hash value?
orientation.correct: A calculated sequence of bits, usually displayed as letters and numbers, produced from particular data such as a file’s contents. It is also called a digest.
distractors: A randomly chosen name with no relationship to the contents.
An encrypted copy that always contains every original byte.
A guarantee that no other possible input can have the same result.
orientation.answer: A calculated sequence of bits, usually displayed as letters and numbers, produced from particular data such as a file’s contents. It is also called a digest.
orientation.teach: A program reads the supplied contents and applies a specified hash calculation. The displayed letters and numbers represent that calculation’s result. The same method and exactly the same bytes give the same result. It is not a random choice, and uniqueness is not guaranteed.
orientation.example: A publisher computes a value for its original file. Your computer computes a value for your downloaded copy. You compare those two values to check the contents.
orientation.context: A private report is saved on a student’s laptop. Later, a separate downloaded installer is checked against a trusted original. These are different tasks: protecting contents from reading and comparing contents for changes.
orientation.purpose: Compute or evaluate a summary of contents so it can be compared with a trusted reference. For a downloaded file, the purpose is to check whether its contents match the original; this does not hide the file or by itself prove who published it.

walkthrough.starting: A downloaded file and a digest supplied through a trusted source for the original file.
walkthrough.operation: A hash program reads the downloaded file’s bytes and performs the hash calculation on them.
walkthrough.result: A fixed-length sequence of bits called a digest, commonly displayed as letters and digits. The digest is a separate computed value, not a replacement for the file.
walkthrough.use: A person or program compares the computed digest with the trusted reference. Different digests mean different contents. A match supports a content match under the hash’s security assumptions; it does not alone prove that the file is safe or who published it.
walkthrough.workedExample: A file containing exactly the text “Amount: 10” has SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) digest 8c8b27520e4a1ce517751f52fff50a3473edc4a9f1cedefcd4e2c379ac9ce0f8. A file containing exactly “Amount: 90” has digest e24d0dad16f71dd46ada00ca89aa14fc46afe38f8907c1d93b7af14c6ff785ac. If the first digest is the publisher’s trusted reference but the download produces the second, the contents differ. The program compares these values; neither value is decrypted to recover the text. These example files have no trailing newline.

timeline.event: Transfers the file to your computer. A download by itself does not imply that a separate reference-hash comparison has happened.

orientation.q: Does calculating the file’s hash normally hide or replace the original file?
orientation.correct: No; it computes a result while the original contents remain readable unless separately protected
distractors: Yes; calculating a hash automatically encrypts the file
Yes; the original must always be deleted

A file containing exactly “Amount: 90” has digest e24d0dad16f71dd46ada00ca89aa14fc46afe38f8907c1d93b7af14c6ff785ac. If the first digest is the publisher’s trusted reference but the download produces the second, the contents differ. The program compares these values; neither value is decrypted to recover the text. These example files have no trailing newline.

walkthrough.workedExample: A file containing exactly the text “Amount: 10” has SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) digest 8c8b27520e4a1ce517751f52fff50a3473edc4a9f1cedefcd4e2c379ac9ce0f8. A file containing exactly “Amount: 90” has digest e24d0dad16f71dd46ada00ca89aa14fc46afe38f8907c1d93b7af14c6ff785ac. If the first digest is the publisher’s trusted reference but the download produces the second, the contents differ. The program compares these values; neither value is decrypted to recover the text. These example files have no trailing newline.

28.object: Customers cannot use a website because an attacker occupies its connection-handling capacity.
28.location: The web server and the network or application connections it handles.
28.purpose: Keep the service usable for legitimate customers.
28.action: SYN floods target connection setup; Slowloris holds web requests incomplete. Match mitigation to the exhausted resource rather than assuming every attack needs enormous bandwidth.

29.object: A website accepts user input, queries a database, and displays results in a browser.
29.location: The application, database query, browser output, and potentially the program’s memory.
29.purpose: Keep input from becoming unintended instructions at the relevant interpreter or memory boundary.
29.action: Parameterized queries address SQL (Structured Query Language) injection; safe output handling addresses XSS (Cross Site Scripting); bounds checking and memory safety address buffer overflows. The flaws affect different places.

32.purpose: Understand how information can be captured at the device even when HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) is used.

33.purpose: Reduce unnecessary exposure and enforce appropriate access and execution rules.
33.action: Use standard accounts, patch software, disable unneeded services, configure host protections, and verify required settings. NAC (Network Access Control), GPO (Group Policy Object), endpoint firewalls, and HIPS (Host Intrusion Prevention System) perform different jobs.

hashTimeline.event: Finalizes the original release file. The file’s exact bytes are the contents that recipients should obtain.

hashTimeline.when: Before or when the release is published
hashTimeline.event: Reads the original file and computes a reference hash using a named method such as SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest). The publisher makes that reference available through a trusted release channel.
Transfers the file to your computer. A download by itself does not imply that a separate reference-hash comparison has happened.

hashTimeline.when: You or a configured verification tool initiates checking
hashTimeline.event: Reads the downloaded file’s bytes and computes its hash using the same method as the publisher. It is not comparing the file with itself.
Compares your computed value with the trusted reference value for that exact release. A different version of the legitimate file needs its own reference.

hashTimeline.who: Person or system deciding whether to use the file
hashTimeline.event: Treats the contents as different from the trusted original and investigates or obtains the correct file. The mismatch does not explain whether the cause was corruption, a legitimate edit, or malicious alteration.
Has evidence supporting a content match under the hash’s security assumptions. The match alone is not a guarantee that the file is harmless, or proof of its publisher if the reference was untrusted.

hashTimeline.when: Checking for later changes instead of checking a download
hashTimeline.who: A file-integrity monitoring system or administrator
hashTimeline.event: Keeps a trusted earlier baseline, recalculates the file’s hash later, and compares the new value with that earlier reference. This is a second scenario; not every system performs it automatically.
